title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
天下之材無乎不有顧世之
求者何如耳三代之士多道
德春秋戰國之士多功利兩
漢以後之士多文學其時殊
其材異非天之生之固然也
盖上以是求之則下以是應
===
之有不能是者皆變遷以從
之耳我
國家自
太祖高皇帝設科目以求道德文
學之士
列聖相承百年于茲士以道德文
應之而文

其材異非天之生之固然也
蓋上以是求之則下以是應
之有不能是者皆變遷以從

國家自
太祖高皇帝設科目以求道德文
學之士
列聖相承百千年茲士以道德文

會試錄序

天下之材，無乎不有，顧世之求者何如耳。三代之士多道德，春秋戰國之士多功利，兩漢以後之士多文學。其時殊，其材異，非天之生之固然也。盖上以是求之，則下以是應之；有不能是者，皆變遷以從之耳。

我國家自太祖高皇帝設科目，以求道德文學之士，列聖相承，百年于茲。士以道德文應之，而文
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

There is no kind of talent lacking in the world; it depends only on what those seeking talent in a given age look for. Scholars of the Three Dynasties excelled chiefly in moral virtue; scholars of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, chiefly in achievement and advantage; and scholars from the two Han dynasties onward, chiefly in literary learning. Their times differed, and their talents differed, but this was not because Heaven had endowed them with fixed differences at birth. Rather, when those above seek a particular quality, those below respond with that quality. Those unable to do so all change themselves to conform.

In our dynasty, since Emperor Taizu Gao established the examination system to seek scholars of moral virtue and literary learning, successive sage emperors have carried it forward for a hundred years down to the present. Scholars have responded with moral virtue and literary accomplishment, and literary …

成化十七年春，復當科試之期，禮部侍郎臣洪謨、臣一夔以考試官請。上命學士臣溥、臣獻往蒞其事。同考則侍講臣音、臣傑，脩撰臣瀚、臣寬、臣遷、臣彦，編脩臣良、臣臣、臣禔，右給事中臣晟，給事中臣中錫，員外郎臣憲，署員外郎臣濬淵，主事臣裕。監試則御史臣介、臣祥，皆遴選以充。于時天下士來就試者四千□□等監內外百
translation_en:
… □□ bringing the people to the conditions of the ages of Tang and Yu [?], leaving their names in the historical annals, and becoming renowned ministers of their age—how could they possibly be counted on one’s fingers?
In the spring of the seventeenth year of Chenghua [1481], the time for the examination came around again. The Vice Ministers of Rites, your servants Hongmo and Yikui, requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded the Academicians, your servants Pu and Xian, to go and preside over the proceedings. The Associate Examiners were the Expositors-in-waiting, your servants Yin and Jie; the Senior Compilers, your servants Han, Kuan, Qian, and Yan; the Junior Compilers, your servants Liang, Chen [?], and Ti; the Supervising Secretary of the Right, your servant Sheng; the Supervising Secretary, your servant Zhongxi; the Vice Director, your servant Xian; the Acting Vice Director, your servant Junyuan; and the Secretary, your servant Yu. Supervising the examination were the Censors, your servants Jie and Xiang. All were carefully selected to fill these posts. At that time, scholars from throughout the realm who came to sit the examination numbered four thousand □□. … and others supervised affairs inside and outside, with all … [?]

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
無事咸矢心竭誠防範加密
三試既畢遵
制額取其文之中式者三百人
爰列其名氏及表其文之尤
粹者彙而成錄臣濫竽主考
當有序以
進蓋臣少居山見山之木若雲
===
然養以雨露之深培以歲月
之久比比皆材者而亦未始
無不材者襍其間欲作室者
必命匠氏於是乎掄之匠氏
徧觀而諦視其材者取之其
不材與夫材而未中度者則
皆棄之矣間有堅其外而朽

無事，咸矢心竭誠，防範加密。三試既畢，遵制額，取其文之中式者三百人。爰列其名氏，及表其文之尤粹者，彙而成錄。臣濫竽主考，當有序以進。
蓋臣少居山，見山之木若雲然，養以雨露之深，培以歲月之久，比比皆材者，而亦未始無不材者襍其間。欲作室者，必命匠氏於是乎掄之。匠氏徧觀而諦視，其材者取之，其不材與夫材而未中度者，則皆棄之矣。間有堅其外而朽
translation_en:
…without incident. All pledged their whole hearts and utmost sincerity, and precautions were further tightened. When the three examination sessions were complete, we observed the quota prescribed by imperial decree and selected three hundred men whose compositions met the standard. We then listed their names and singled out their finest compositions, compiling them into this record. Having unworthily occupied the position of chief Examiner, I, your servant, ought to provide a preface for submission to the throne.
In my youth I lived in the mountains, where I saw trees massed like clouds. Nourished abundantly by rain and dew and nurtured over many years, trees fit for timber stood everywhere; yet trees unfit for timber were also interspersed among them. Anyone wishing to build a house would certainly instruct a carpenter to select from among these trees. The carpenter would survey them thoroughly and examine them closely, taking those fit for timber and rejecting both those that were unfit and those that, though usable as timber, did not yet meet the required dimensions. Occasionally there were trees hard on the outside but rotten …

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
上干惡其□□而美其膚者則
非匠氏一時目力之所能辨
也必待斲削之乃始見而亦
不免於棄耳具能倖而為棟
梁榱桷者不亦罕哉今士荷
國家作養之恩非一日皆以道
德文學應
===
上而起既取之於今矣其用之於
後也可待由是入官必使德
與文副實與華稱凡異日之
所行皆不負今日之所取則
士而大夫而卿而公如前所
謂致堯舜措唐虞以為一代
名臣斯偉矣不然今雖羣
alt_text:
士于匪其材而美其膚者則
非匠氏一時目力之所能辨
也必待斲削之乃始見而亦
不免於棄耳其能偉而為棟
梁榱桷者不亦罕哉今士荷
國家作養之恩非一日皆以道
德文學應
===
上而起既取之於今矣其用之於
後也可待由是入官必使德
與文副實與華稱凡異日之
所行皆不負今日之所取則
士而大夫而卿而公如前所
謂致堯舜措唐虞以為一代
名臣者偉矣不然今雖幸
punctuated: 上干，惡其□□而美其膚者，則非匠氏一時目力之所能辨也。必待斲削之，乃始見，而亦不免於棄耳。具能倖而為棟梁榱桷者，不亦罕哉？今士荷國家作養之恩非一日，皆以道德文學應上而起。既取之於今矣，其用之於後也可待。由是入官，必使德與文副，實與華稱。凡異日之所行，皆不負今日之所取，則士而大夫而卿而公，如前所謂致堯舜、措唐虞，以為一代名臣，斯偉矣！不然，今雖羣
translation_en:
…[The opening characters 上干 are unclear.] Those whose □□ is defective but whose outer surface is fine cannot be distinguished by a craftsman’s momentary visual inspection. Only when they are hewn and trimmed do their defects become apparent, and they too cannot escape rejection. Surely it is rare for such timber to slip through by good fortune and become ridgepoles, beams, or rafters [?].

For more than a day, scholars have received the state’s gracious nurture and cultivation. All rise in response to the sovereign’s call, presenting their moral character and literary learning. Having now been selected, they may look forward to employment hereafter. Upon entering office by this route, they must ensure that their virtue matches their literary accomplishments and that their substance accords with their outward brilliance. If everything they do in future lives up to the grounds on which they were selected today, they may advance from scholars to grand masters, to ministers, and to dukes. As stated above, they may bring their sovereign to the stature of Yao and Shun and establish the good government of Tang and Yu, becoming renowned ministers of their age. How splendid that would be! Otherwise, although today they are gathered together …

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
□後安可保不爲人所棄哉
溥等掄材者也斵材者欲用
之爲棟梁榱桷之具其亦相
與謹之
嘉議大夫太常寺卿兼翰林
院學士徐溥謹序
alt_text:
擭安可以不爲人所棄哉
溥等掄材者也斲材者欲用
之爲棟梁榱桷之具其亦相
與謹之
嘉議大夫太常寺卿兼翰林
院學士徐溥謹序
punctuated:
□，後安可保不爲人所棄哉？溥等掄材者也，斵材者欲用之爲棟梁榱桷之具，其亦相與謹之。
嘉議大夫、太常寺卿兼翰林院學士徐溥謹序。
translation_en:
…[illegible character; sense uncertain]—how can one be sure that later one will not be cast aside by others? We, Xu Pu and his colleagues, are selectors of timber; those who hew it wish to use it as ridgepoles, beams, and rafters. Let us all exercise care in this together.
Preface respectfully written by Xu Pu, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
四書
出門如見大賓使民如承大祭
執其兩端用其中於民
君子之所爲衆人固不識也
易
大亨貞无咎而天下隨時
有孚威如終吉
剛柔者立本者也
===
知幾其神乎君子上交不諂下交不瀆其
知幾乎幾者動之微吉之先見者也
君子見幾而作不俟終日易曰介于
石不終日貞吉介如石焉寧用終日
斷可識矣君子知微知彰知柔知剛
萬夫之望

translation_en:
Four Books
“When going out, conduct yourself as though meeting an honored guest; when employing the people, act as though officiating at a great sacrifice.”
“He grasped the two extremes and applied the mean between them to the people.”
“What the gentleman does, ordinary people indeed do not understand.”

Book of Changes
“Great success; correctness; no blame. All under Heaven follow the times.”
“With sincerity and an awe-inspiring bearing, there will be good fortune in the end.”
“The firm and the yielding are what establish the foundation.”
“To discern the first stirrings of things—is this not spirit-like insight? In his dealings with those above him, the gentleman does not flatter; in his dealings with those below him, he is not disrespectfully familiar. Does he not discern the first stirrings? These stirrings are the faint beginnings of movement, the first signs of good fortune appearing. The gentleman perceives them and acts, without waiting for the day to end. The Book of Changes says: ‘Firm as a rock; without waiting for the day to end; correctness brings good fortune.’ Firm as a rock, why would he need a whole day? The judgment can already be known. The gentleman understands the subtle and the manifest, the yielding and the firm: he is the one to whom the multitude looks.”

Book of Documents
“Make clear the sight of the eyes in all four quarters, and open the hearing of the ears in all four quarters.”
“Among the ghosts and spirits, too, none were without repose; even the birds, beasts, fish, and turtles were all in harmony.”

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
弱繫焉牧民之司邦本之安危繫焉賦斂
也漕運也又
國用京儲所資以足焉者也是四者誠非當
今之細務矣
祖宗之時府衛將校皆拔自行伍爵必驗其功
績任必擇其智勇何有於典兵之非人也
夫何承平既久襲蔭皆紈袴之流干城付
膏粱之胤鞍馬弓矢之未習戰陣韜畧之
未閑緩急其可倚邪掌兵柄者不可不加
===
之意也必也申武學之教不視為虛文設
武舉之科以驗其實用冒功者必罰失機
者必罰肆惡而剋下怙恩而養寇者必罰
則典兵者庶乎得其人而兵可振寇可禦
矣
宗之時藩臬守令多出於
簡命職必量其材能進不拘於科目何有於
牧民之非人也夫何邇年以来超遷惟取
於資格考覈或采於愛憎視催科為能官

未聞緩急其可倚邪掌兵柄者不可不加
之意也必也申武學之教不視為虛文設

者必罰肆惡而剋下怙恩而養寇者必罰

===
矣
宗之時藩臬守令多於
簡命職必量其材能進不拘於科目何有於
牧民之非人也夫何邇年以來超遷惟取
於資格考覈或采於愛憎視催科為能官
punctuated:
弱繫焉，牧民之司，邦本之安危繫焉。賦斂也，漕運也，又國用京儲所資以足焉者也。是四者，誠非當今之細務矣。
祖宗之時，府衛將校皆拔自行伍，爵必驗其功績，任必擇其智勇，何有於典兵之非人也？夫何承平既久，襲蔭皆紈袴之流，干城付膏粱之胤，鞍馬弓矢之未習，戰陣韜畧之未閑，緩急其可倚邪？掌兵柄者不可不加之意也。必也申武學之教，不視為虛文；設武舉之科，以驗其實用。冒功者必罰，失機者必罰，肆惡而剋下、怙恩而養寇者必罰。則典兵者庶乎得其人，而兵可振，寇可禦矣。
宗之時，藩臬守令多出於簡命，職必量其材能，進不拘於科目，何有於牧民之非人也？夫何邇年以来，超遷惟取於資格，考覈或采於愛憎，視催科為能官，
translation_en:
…weakness depends upon them; upon the officials charged with governing the people depends the security or peril of the foundation of the state. Tax collection and grain transport, moreover, provide the resources needed to meet state expenditure and replenish the capital’s granaries. These four matters are certainly no minor concerns of the present day.
In the time of the ancestral emperors, commanders and officers of the chief military commissions and guards were all promoted from the ranks. Noble rank was awarded only after verification of their achievements, and appointments were made by selecting for intelligence and courage. How could command of troops have fallen to unsuitable men? Yet now, after so long a period of peace, those who succeed to hereditary privileges are all pampered sons of wealthy families, and the defense of the realm is entrusted to the offspring of luxury. Unpracticed in horsemanship and archery, and unfamiliar with battle formations and military strategy, can they be relied upon in an emergency? Those who wield military authority must give this their attention. They must reinforce instruction in the military schools, rather than treating it as an empty formality, and establish military examinations to test practical ability. Those who falsely claim military merit must be punished; those who miss an opportunity in battle must be punished; and those who wantonly perpetrate evil and oppress their subordinates, or rely on imperial favor and allow bandits to flourish, must be punished. Then perhaps suitable men will command the troops, the army can be reinvigorated, and bandits can be repelled.
In the time of the ancestral sovereigns [?], provincial administration commissioners and surveillance commissioners, prefects, and magistrates were mostly appointed through imperial selection. Their abilities were always weighed before they were assigned office, and advancement was not restricted by examination credentials. How could the governance of the people have fallen to unsuitable men? Yet why, in recent years, have exceptional promotions depended solely on formal qualifications and seniority, while evaluations sometimes reflect personal affection or dislike, and officials are judged capable for pressing the collection of taxes…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
以媚竈爲捷徑人民何所賴邪掌銓衡者
不可不加之意也必也不惑於即墨之毀
言日至致察於膠東之戶口偽增苛虐者
必黜罷軟者必黜卑順以趨名刻削以足
欲者必黜則循良者庶乎得其人而事不
煩民不擾矣往者吳楚諸郡賦斂有藝而
田野富庶故粟米之實於倉廩以備
國用者陳陳相因豈非周文襄經畫之善邪
今絲縷布帛亦征以粟而官糶之法復行
===
於市出納之際稅長里胥競容其奸弊不
可勝言矣蓋折銀之惠民久賴之此在職
巡撫者因舊法而推行之以順民心一遇
歲凶又必爲之從實蠲免使無追賠之害
則民之病庶其少瘳乎往者齊魯諸水流
通無壅舟楫易達餽餉之運於漕河以
充京儲者源源不絕豈非陳恭襄區處之
善邪今支兌轉輸既盡其力而私貸之息
復倍於人朘削之餘其財與力于茲兩竭

少婣竄爲捷徑人民何所賴邪掌銓衡者
不可不加之意也必也不惑於即墨之毀
言日至數察於膠東之戶口偽增苛虐者
必黜罷軟者必咻〔使順以趨名刻削以足〕
欲者必黜則爲民者庶乎得其人而事不
煩民不擾矣往者吳楚諸郡賦斂有藝而
田野富庶蘇界之實於倉廩以備
國用者陳陳相因豈非周文襄經畫之善邪
今絲縷布帛亦征以粟而官糴之法復行
===
於市出納之際稅長里胥競容其奸弊不
可勝言矣蓋折銀之惠民久賴之此在職
巡撫者因舊法而推行之以順民心一遇
歲凶又必爲之從實蠲免使無追陪之害
則民之病庶乎少瘳乎往者齊魯諸水流
通無壅舟楫易達　饋餉之運於漕河以
充京儲者源源不絕豈非陳恭襄區處之
邪今支兌轉輸既盡其力而私貸之息
又從人船剝之餘其財與力于茲兩竭
punctuated:
以媚竈爲捷徑，人民何所賴邪？掌銓衡者不可不加之意也。必也不惑於即墨之毀言日至，致察於膠東之戶口偽增。苛虐者必黜，罷軟者必黜，卑順以趨名、刻削以足欲者必黜，則循良者庶乎得其人，而事不煩、民不擾矣。
往者吳楚諸郡，賦斂有藝，而田野富庶，故粟米之實於倉廩以備國用者，陳陳相因，豈非周文襄經畫之善邪？今絲縷布帛亦征以粟，而官糶之法復行於市。出納之際，稅長里胥競容其奸，弊不可勝言矣。蓋折銀之惠，民久賴之。此在職巡撫者因舊法而推行之，以順民心；一遇歲凶，又必爲之從實蠲免，使無追賠之害，則民之病庶其少瘳乎？
往者齊魯諸水，流通無壅，舟楫易達，餽餉之運於漕河以充京儲者，源源不絕，豈非陳恭襄區處之善邪？今支兌轉輸既盡其力，而私貸之息復倍於人，朘削之餘，其財與力于茲兩竭
translation_en:
…and regard currying favor with the powerful as a shortcut to advancement—on whom, then, can the people rely? Those responsible for selecting and appointing officials must give this their attention. They must not be misled by the daily arrival of slanderous reports about Jimo, and must closely scrutinize the falsely inflated household and population figures for Jiaodong. The harsh and oppressive must be dismissed; the weak and ineffectual must be dismissed; those who seek a reputation through servile compliance, or satisfy their desires by grinding exactions, must be dismissed. Then perhaps genuinely benevolent and upright officials will be found, administrative business will cease to be burdensome, and the people will be free from harassment.
Formerly, in the prefectures of Wu and Chu, taxation had its limits and the countryside was prosperous. Thus grain stored in the granaries for state use accumulated year after year, new stocks following upon old. Was this not due to the sound planning of Zhou Wenxiang? Now even levies on silk thread and cloth are collected in grain, while the practice of selling government grain has again been introduced in the markets. During receipts and disbursements, tax headmen and village clerks vie in giving scope to their frauds; the abuses are beyond recounting. The people have long relied on the benefit of commuting their taxes to silver. It rests with those serving as grand coordinators to extend this established practice in accordance with the people’s wishes. Whenever a bad harvest occurs, they must also grant remissions according to actual conditions, sparing the people the harm of subsequent demands for repayment. Might the people’s suffering then be somewhat relieved?
Formerly, the waterways of Qi and Lu flowed freely without obstruction, and boats could readily pass. Supplies transported along the Grand Canal to replenish the capital’s reserves arrived in an unbroken stream. Was this not due to the sound arrangements of Chen Gongxiang? Now receiving and transferring grain and transporting it onward have already exhausted their strength, while interest on private loans is twice that charged to others. After these exactions, their wealth and strength are both exhausted…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
安竊可勝言矣盖直達之法宋已病之此
夫職漕運者因遺迹而脩治之以順河流
一遇水涸又必使之隨便峙積別為轉般
之計則兵之困庶乎少甦乎於戲政之立
於初也本無不宜政之行於久也不能無
弊非特是四者為然也因其弊而脩其政
則在乎人焉今
聖天子既皆得人而任之矣斡旋化樞圖回治
道廟堂之上必有成筭顧愚何人而敢妄
===
議邪執事幸進教之

〔水衡〕可勝言矣盖直達之法宋已病之此
〔職〕漕運者因遺迹而脩治之以順河流
一遇水涸又必使之隨便峙積別為轉般
之計則兵之〔困於〕〔牽挽〕□乎於戲政之立
於初也本無不宜政之行於久也不能無
弊非特是四者為然也因其弊而脩其政
則在乎人焉今
聖天子既皆得人而任之矣斡旋化樞圖回治
道廟堂之上必有成筭顧愚何人而敢妄
議邪執事辜進教之
punctuated: 安竊可勝言矣！盖直達之法，宋已病之。此夫職漕運者，因遺迹而脩治之，以順河流；一遇水涸，又必使之隨便峙積，別為轉般之計，則兵之困庶乎少甦乎？於戲！政之立於初也，本無不宜；政之行於久也，不能無弊。非特是四者為然也。因其弊而脩其政，則在乎人焉。今聖天子既皆得人而任之矣，斡旋化樞，圖回治道，廟堂之上必有成筭。顧愚何人，而敢妄議邪？執事幸進教之。
translation_en:
…how could this distress be fully recounted [?]? Indeed, the system of direct delivery had already caused hardship under the Song. Those responsible for grain transport [?] should follow the surviving traces of the waterways and repair them so that the rivers flow freely. Whenever the water runs dry, they must also have the grain stockpiled wherever convenient and make separate arrangements for its onward transport. Might the soldiers’ hardship then be somewhat relieved?

Alas! When policies are first established, they are originally appropriate in every respect; when carried out over a long period, they cannot remain free of abuses. This is true of more than just these four matters. To remedy policies in response to their abuses depends upon the people entrusted with them. Now our sagely Son of Heaven has already found suitable men and appointed them all. At court, there must surely be settled plans for directing the workings of transformation and advancing the way of good government. Yet who am I, in my ignorance, to venture rash opinions? I humbly hope that you, Sir, will offer me instruction.

會試錄後序

皇上膺天眷命，嗣承祖宗弘大靈長之業，于茲十有七載。宵旰勵精，誕敷文教，更張弛墜，治具一新，而謂設科求賢，寔惟制治保邦之本，尤惓惓焉。

成化辛丑春二月，適當會試之期，禮部以聞，命臣溥、臣獻往司校文之任，而同考諸執事亦皆遴簡以充。臣等祗奉
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

His Majesty received Heaven’s favor and mandate and succeeded to the vast and enduring enterprise of his imperial ancestors. Seventeen years have now passed. Attending to affairs before dawn and eating late, he has devoted himself tirelessly to governing, broadly disseminated civil instruction, and reformed what had fallen into neglect, renewing all the institutions of government. He considers the establishment of examinations to seek worthy men to be the very foundation of good government and the security of the realm, and has been especially solicitous in this regard.

In the second month of spring in the xinchou year of the Chenghua reign [1481], when the Metropolitan Examination was due, the Ministry of Rites reported the matter to the throne. His Majesty commanded your servants Pu 溥 and Xian 獻 to undertake the assessment of examination essays, and the Associate Examiners were likewise all carefully selected to fill their posts. We, your servants, reverently received…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
是夙夜兢惕更相戒誓毋怠
事毋狥私毋矯情示公毋衒
直干譽毋黜雅崇浮以遺實
才毋厭常喜新以逐時好毋
穿鑿臆說以昧至理毋偏恃
己長以拒衆善有一於此幽
有鬼神將孰欺乎明有物議
===
將安逭乎凡三試既得士如
制又刋其氏名及文之優者為
錄以
進臣敏謹序其後竊惟國家之
有賢才猶天之有日星地之
有山川草木也夫天非日星
則天道晦矣地非山川草木

思夙夜兢惕更相戒誓毋怠
事毋徇私毋矯情示公毋衒
直干譽毋以雅崇浮以遺實
才毋厭常喜新以逐時好毋
穿鑿臆說以昧至理毋偏恃
己長以拒衆善有一於此幽
有鬼神將執敢乎明有物議
將安逭乎凡三試旣得士如
制又刋其氏名及文之優者爲
錄以
進臣　謹序其後竊惟國家之
有賢才猶天之有日星地之
有山川草木也夫天非日星
則天道晦矣地非山川草木
punctuated:
是夙夜兢惕，更相戒誓：毋怠事，毋狥私，毋矯情示公，毋衒直干譽，毋黜雅崇浮以遺實才，毋厭常喜新以逐時好，毋穿鑿臆說以昧至理，毋偏恃己長以拒衆善。有一於此，幽有鬼神，將孰欺乎？明有物議，將安逭乎？凡三試，既得士如制，又刋其氏名及文之優者為錄，以進。
臣敏謹序其後。竊惟國家之有賢才，猶天之有日星，地之有山川草木也。夫天非日星，則天道晦矣；地非山川草木，
translation_en:
…Thus we remained vigilant and apprehensive day and night, repeatedly admonishing one another and pledging: do not neglect your duties; do not indulge private interests; do not feign impartiality; do not parade uprightness to seek praise; do not reject refined writing and exalt superficiality, thereby overlooking genuine talent; do not tire of the familiar and delight in novelty merely to pursue contemporary fashions; do not obscure ultimate principles with strained interpretations and conjectural explanations; and do not rely exclusively on your own strengths and reject the merits of others. If we committed any one of these faults, in the unseen realm there would be ghosts and spirits—whom could we deceive? In the visible realm there would be public criticism—how could we escape it? After all three examination sessions, having selected men in accordance with the regulations, we also printed their names and the best of their compositions as a record, to be presented to the throne.
Your servant Min respectfully appends this postface. I humbly consider that a state’s possession of worthy talent is like heaven’s possession of the sun and stars, or earth’s possession of mountains, rivers, plants, and trees. Without the sun and stars, the Way of Heaven would be obscured; without mountains, rivers, plants, and trees, earth…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
則地道虧矣國家非賢才則
治道否矣然天地之運以氣
國家之治以理賢才理之所
寓也理正則氣亦正焉自古
聖帝明王之有天下不患三
光之弗寧寒暑之弗節水土
之弗平鳥獸草木之弗咸若
===
惟患所以輔吾治者無賢才
耳故曰所寶惟賢此之謂歟
學校賢才之所聚也科目賢

===
惟患所以輔吾治者無賢才
耳故曰所寶惟賢此之謂歟
學校賢才之所聚也科目賢
才之所出也夫士初養於學

punctuated:
則地道虧矣，國家非賢才則治道否矣。然天地之運以氣，國家之治以理，賢才，理之所寓也。理正則氣亦正焉。自古聖帝明王之有天下，不患三光之弗寧、寒暑之弗節、水土之弗平、鳥獸草木之弗咸若，惟患所以輔吾治者無賢才耳。故曰：「所寶惟賢。」此之謂歟？

學校，賢才之所聚也；科目，賢才之所出也。夫士初養於學，所習者孔孟之書，其學同也；所談者伊周之事業，其志同也。茲由科目簡拔而出，對策
translation_en:
…then the Way of Earth would be impaired; without worthy talent in the state, the Way of government would be obstructed. Yet Heaven and Earth operate through vital energy (qi), while the state is governed through principle (li). Worthy men are where principle resides. When principle is properly ordered, vital energy is also properly ordered. Since antiquity, when sage emperors and enlightened kings possessed All under Heaven, their concern was not that the three luminaries—the sun, moon, and stars—might be unsettled, that cold and heat might fail to follow their seasons, that waters and lands might be out of order, or that birds, beasts, grasses, and trees might not all thrive in harmony. Their sole concern was that there might be no worthy men to assist their governance. Thus it is said: “Only the worthy are to be treasured.” Is this not what those words mean?

Schools are where worthy talent gathers; the examinations are where worthy talent emerges. When scholars are first nurtured in the schools, they study the writings of Confucius and Mencius: their learning is the same. They discuss the achievements of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou: their aspirations are the same. Now, selected and advanced through the examinations, they come forth to answer policy questions…

translation_en: …in the great court, and are granted the designation of metropolitan graduate (jinshi), their honor is likewise the same. Yet when they take office and undertake government, gradually advancing into positions of trust, differences begin to appear among them. Why is this? Their desire for profit and official emoluments has led them astray. They must ensure that their conduct in prominence does not depart from the principles they upheld in obscurity. Whatever duties they are assigned according to their abilities, they must strive to serve their sovereign loyally and bestow benefits upon the people. In this way, shaping and assisting the work of government, they may become eminent ministers of the state, quietly commanding respect. People will look up to them as to the towering heights of Mount Tai and other lofty peaks, and admire them as auspicious portents, splendid as the felicitous star and the numinous fungus. This would bring glory to the realm and be a cause for rejoicing in our cultural tradition. But if any abandon what they have learned to indulge their appetites, scorn ritual propriety and undermine established standards, thus betraying their designation as worthy and talented men, they are no different from weeds among the seedlings or shriveled grains among the millet. The multitude casts them aside, and gentlemen…

We have received Heaven’s mandate. □□ [?] the years of Xia; may the years of Yin likewise not be cut short.
If you have good plans and good counsels, enter and report them to your sovereign within the palace.

Book of Odes
That man is an outstanding worthy of the state.
What hour of the night is it? The night is not yet half spent. In the light of the courtyard torches, the lords arrive, their carriage bells jingling.
A mandate came from Heaven, bestowing its charge upon King Wen. In Zhou, in the capital, the woman who continued your line was from Shen. The eldest daughter went to be married and gave birth to King Wu, the great.
Ah, illustrious ancestor! These blessings follow in due order, bestowed repeatedly without limit, reaching you here. We have set out clear wine; grant us the fulfillment of our hopes. There is also harmoniously seasoned broth, duly prepared and balanced. We approach and present the offerings without words [?]; there is no contention. Grant us long life, venerable old age without limit. With leather-bound hubs [?] and ornamented crossbars, the eight carriage bells ring out as we approach and offer sacrifice. The mandate we have received is vast and great. From Heaven descend peace and abundant harvests, rich in grain. Come, approach; come, partake! Send down blessings without limit. Look upon our winter and autumn sacrifices, presented by the descendant of Tang.

第叁場，策五道。

問：聖人作民元后，必有垂世立教之制。若我太祖高皇帝之《大誥三編》，太宗文皇帝之《為善陰騭》《孝順事實》，宣宗章皇帝之《五倫書》，皆炳如六經，家傳而人誦之矣。至若《大明律》一書，所以禁奸暴、遏亂畧、象典刑以弼教化者也。當時雖命臣下刋修，而實出宸衷裁决，故卓冠千古之刑書，永垂百王之法度矣。試與諸士子講之。先儒云：「以五禮之有春秋，猶法律之有斷例。」然則五經之有《春秋》，猶法律之有斷例，果若是班乎？

Delaying official documents beyond the prescribed time.
Failing to drill soldiers.
Manufacturing or construction that does not conform to regulations.

Third Session: Five Policy Questions.

Question: When a sage becomes the sovereign of the people, he must establish institutions that transmit instruction to later ages. Such are the Three Compilations of the Grand Pronouncements of our Emperor Taizu Gao; Doing Good and Hidden Merit and True Accounts of Filial Obedience of Emperor Taizong Wen; and the Book of the Five Human Relationships of Emperor Xuanzong Zhang. All shine as brightly as the Six Classics; they are handed down in every household and recited by everyone. As for the Great Ming Code, it prohibits wickedness and violence, restrains disorder and depredation, and sets forth the established punishments to assist moral instruction. Although ministers were then commanded to edit and revise it, its decisions in fact proceeded from the imperial mind. Thus it stands preeminent among the penal codes of all ages and will endure forever as a legal standard for successive sovereigns.

Let us discuss it with you candidates. An earlier Confucian scholar said: “The Five Rites having the Spring and Autumn Annals is like laws having precedents for judgments.” [?] Is it, then, truly the case that the Five Classics having the Spring and Autumn Annals is like laws having precedents for judgments [?]?

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
兵家者同不數也昔聖人因以制刑
漢世獨引經而斷獄律之書始於何代
而律之名何所取義歟今之律與前歷
代之律可詳言之歟今律有五刑而虞
周皆有五刑周又有八刑今律有八議
而周有八辟今律有三流而虞有五流
今律有八字而隋律亦有八字可究其
異同之詳歟今律大抵皆因唐律而損
益之亦可舉其槩歟夫讀書而不讀律

大明律乃
聖朝之制作與前三詔三書同播之天下而垂

心於是矣詳著于篇以觀用世之學

缺一而禮樂尤切於人身未嘗斯須去
之自覇秦之興獨任刑政而禮樂蕩廢
漢因陋就簡禮樂無聞焉稚樂文章

punctuated:
兵家者同不數也。昔聖人因以制刑，漢世獨引經而斷獄。律之書始於何代，而律之名何所取義歟？今之律與前歷代之律，可詳言之歟？今律有五刑，而虞、周皆有五刑，周又有八刑；今律有八議，而周有八辟；今律有三流，而虞有五流；今律有八字，而隋律亦有八字。可究其異同之詳歟？今律大抵皆因唐律而損益之，亦可舉其槩歟？夫讀書而不讀律，古人嘗有致君無術之說。況今之所謂《大明律》，乃聖朝之制作，與前三詔三書同播之天下而垂諸萬世者也。諸士子行將入仕，必嘗究心於是矣。詳著于篇，以觀用世之學。
問：古之言治者必曰禮、樂、刑、政，四者不可缺一，而禮樂尤切於人身，未嘗斯須去之。自覇秦之興，獨任刑政，而禮樂蕩廢。漢因陋就簡，禮樂無聞焉。稚樂文章
translation_en:
…military writers are alike and are not counted [?]. In antiquity, the sages drew upon this to establish punishments; in Han times, they alone [?] cited the Classics to decide legal cases. In what age did written penal codes originate, and from what meaning was the designation lü, “statutes,” derived? Can you discuss in detail the present code and the codes of preceding dynasties? The present code has five punishments, and both Yu and Zhou likewise had five punishments; Zhou also had eight punishments. The present code has eight deliberations granting special consideration, while Zhou had eight provisions for special consideration. The present code has three degrees of exile, while Yu had five degrees of exile. The present code has eight characters [?], and the Sui code likewise had eight characters [?]. Can you investigate their similarities and differences in detail? The present code largely follows the Tang code, with additions and deletions. Can you also outline these? Regarding those who read books but do not read the statutes, the ancients once said that they lacked the means to guide their ruler. Moreover, what is now called the Great Ming Code is a creation of our sagely dynasty, promulgated throughout the realm together with the three edicts and three books mentioned above, and handed down for ten thousand generations. You candidates will shortly enter official service and must already have devoted thought to these matters. Set out your answers in detail so that we may assess your learning for practical service.
Question: Those who discussed government in antiquity invariably spoke of ritual, music, punishments, and administration. None of these four could be dispensed with, while ritual and music bore particularly closely upon personal conduct and were never to be abandoned even for a moment. With the rise of the hegemonic Qin, reliance was placed solely on punishments and administration, and ritual and music fell into complete neglect. The Han perpetuated crude practices and made do with simplified arrangements; ritual and music went unheard of. “Young music” and ceremonial forms [?] …

punctuated: □□之郊聲朝只而已。偏州下邑，□□竽管簘，至舉莫識其器，何有於樂乎？縱曰有樂，亦不過胡部、俗部導欲增悲者爾。是四者之中，樂獨久廢，豈後世之為治宜無待於樂乎？我國朝禮樂之制，可謂備矣，然猶未盡復古。昔人謂禮樂積德百年而後興，自有國迄今百有餘年，四時順序，八風不奸，作樂以宣天地之和，此其時乎？古樂之見諸《周官》者，《雲門》、《大卷》、《大咸》、《大磬》、《大夏》、《大濩》、《大武》而已。又有所謂《立本》、《下謀》、《屬續》、《九淵》者，誰氏之樂也？古樂廢於秦矣，漢乃有宗廟樂，有房中樂，有神樂；唐有雅樂，有燕樂，有凱樂；宋有乾德雅樂，有萬國朝天樂，有平晉樂，有大安樂，有大晟樂。可得而詳之歟？樂書既亡，後世知□□鮮矣。若王朴、李照之所定，范鎮、司馬光之論□□□，蔡元定之所著，可得而言之，
translation_en:
…□□, sounds for the suburban sacrifices and the court [?], and nothing more. In remote prefectures and lesser towns, □□, the yu mouth organ, pipes, and xiao flute [?]—indeed, no one even recognizes the instruments. How could there be music? Even if one says there is music, it amounts only to foreign and popular repertories that stir desire and deepen sorrow. Thus, among these four elements, music alone has long fallen into disuse. Can it be that government in later ages should have no need of music? Our dynasty’s institutions of rites and music may be called comprehensive, yet they have not fully restored ancient practice. People of old said that rites and music arise only after virtue has accumulated for a hundred years. More than a hundred years have now passed since the founding of the dynasty. The four seasons follow their proper sequence, and the winds from the eight directions cause no disorder. Is this not the time to create music to give expression to the harmony of Heaven and Earth?

The ancient musical works recorded in the Offices of Zhou are simply Cloud Gate (Yunmen), Great Unfolding (Dajuan), Great Harmony (Daxian), Great Chime (Daqing) [?], Great Xia (Daxia), Great Deliverance (Dahuo), and Great Martial Dance (Dawu). There are also those called Establishing the Foundation (Liben), Lower Counsel (Xiamou) [?], Continuation (Shuxu), and Nine Depths (Jiuyuan). Whose music were these? Ancient music fell into disuse under the Qin. The Han, however, had music for the ancestral temples, music of the inner chambers, and music for the spirits. The Tang had elegant ritual music, banquet music, and music of triumph. The Song had elegant ritual music of the Qiande era, music of the Myriad States Paying Court to the Son of Heaven, music of the Pacification of Jin, music of Great Peace, and music of Great Splendor. Can these be explained in detail? Since the writings on music have been lost, few in later ages have understood □□. As for what Wang Pu and Li Zhao established, the discussions of Fan Zhen and Sima Guang □□□, and the writings of Cai Yuanding, can these be expounded …

以四達不悖斯須不去移風易俗天下
和平以復唐虞三代之治必有道矣幸
悉陳之毋曰以俟君子
問三代之時教養法備士之由於學校者
才無不全其用於世治無不善然伊尹
之舉於畎畝傅說之舉於版築太公望

或起刀筆文帝未遑禮樂而申韓黃老
之術更進迭用考其治效亦秩然可觀

元帝雅尚儒術貢薛韋匡迭用為相而
漢業衰焉豈學校之設果無關於治道
而人才之成有不係於教養歟光武臨

參酌百王之樂，以成一代之制，以四達不悖，斯須不去，移風易俗，天下和平，以復唐虞三代之治，必有道矣。幸悉陳之，毋曰以俟君子。
問：三代之時，教養法備，士之由於學校者，才無不全；其用於世，治無不善。然伊尹之舉於畎畝，傅說之舉於版築，太公望之舉於釣，盡當世之賢，誠未有及之者。三子者何以不出於學歟？漢承秦弊，高祖以溺冠嫚罵之資，而其臣或任智數，或起刀筆。文帝未遑禮樂，而申韓黃老之術更進迭用，考其治效，亦秩然可觀。武帝勸學興禮，表章六經，而海內虛耗；元帝雅尚儒術，貢薛韋匡迭用為相，而漢業衰焉。豈學校之設果無關於治道，而人才之成有不係於教養歟？光武臨雍拜老，尊禮師傅；唐太宗大召名儒，增廣生員，而先儒謂其未知所以
translation_en:
…To weigh and draw upon the music of the many kings in order to establish the institutions of a dynasty, so that it reaches in all four directions without discord and is never forsaken even for an instant, transforms customs, and brings peace and harmony throughout the realm, thereby restoring the good government of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties—there must surely be a way to accomplish this. Please set it forth fully; do not say that it must await a gentleman of virtue.
Question: During the Three Dynasties, the methods of educating and nurturing men were fully developed. Scholars who came through the schools were complete in their abilities, and when employed in the world, invariably governed well. Yet Yi Yin was raised to office from the fields, Fu Yue from building rammed-earth walls, and Taigong Wang from fishing; among all the worthy men of their times, truly none equaled them. Why did these three men not come from the schools? The Han inherited the abuses of the Qin. Gaozu had a disposition that led him to urinate in scholars’ caps and revile them, while his ministers either relied on clever stratagems or rose from clerical work. Emperor Wen had no leisure for rites and music, while the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, and of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi, were advanced and employed in turn. Yet an examination of the results of his government reveals an orderliness worthy of admiration. Emperor Wu encouraged learning, promoted ritual, and gave prominence to the Six Classics, yet the realm was depleted. Emperor Yuan habitually esteemed Confucian learning, and Gong, Xue, Wei, and Kuang were appointed successively as chancellors, yet the Han imperial enterprise declined. Could the establishment of schools really have no bearing on the way of governing, and could the development of talented men be independent of their education and nurture? Emperor Guangwu visited the imperial academy and bowed to the elders, honoring teachers and tutors with due ceremony. Emperor Taizong of Tang summoned renowned Confucian scholars in great numbers and expanded student enrollment. Yet earlier Confucian scholars said that they did not understand the means by which…

此亦不知所謂教者果何事歟宋慶曆
間始詔天下立學前此固未盛也而韓
范諸賢胥此焉出厥後蘇湖之學人稱
其得人或以淵篤稱或以純明著或以

取則三代公卿大臣非由此不任郡邑

punctuated:
此亦不知所謂教者果何事歟？宋慶曆間，始詔天下立學，前此固未盛也，而韓范諸賢胥此焉出。厥後蘇湖之學，人稱其得人，或以淵篤稱，或以純明著，或以直溫顯，或以簡諒聞。其所以教之養之者，果有得於三代之法否乎？今之學宮徧天下，而人皆知務學。列聖相承，深仁厚澤已漸摩百年，良法美意悉取則三代。公卿大臣非由此不任，郡邑守令非出此不選，宜乎人才盛而治化成矣。然士知自重者，每不屑就夫師儒，而為祿仕者輙不留心於教事，豈法之在人，尚亦有鼓舞而風勵之者乎？歷考古今學校人才治道盛衰隆替之故，不能無可疑焉，故從諸生質之，願推其本原而斟酌其所當行者。

古者任土作貢，揚州之域，厥田下下。今吳下諸郡、湖諸郡，皆揚州之故域。仲雍
translation_en:
…Did they, too, not understand what teaching actually entails? Only during the Qingli era of the Song was an edict first issued establishing schools throughout the realm. Before this, schools certainly had not flourished, yet such worthies as Han and Fan all emerged in that earlier period. Subsequently, the schools of Suzhou and Huzhou were praised for producing worthy men: some were renowned for depth and steadfastness, some distinguished for purity and discernment, some eminent for uprightness and gentleness, and some known for simplicity and trustworthiness. Did the methods by which these men were taught and nurtured truly capture something of the methods of the Three Dynasties?

Today, schools extend throughout the realm, and everyone knows to apply himself to learning. Our successive sagely emperors have nurtured the people with profound benevolence and abundant beneficence for a hundred years; their excellent institutions and admirable intentions all take the Three Dynasties as their model. High ministers and great officials are not appointed unless they have passed through these schools, and prefects and county magistrates are not selected unless they come from them. It should follow that talented men abound and good government and moral transformation are achieved. Yet scholars who value their own standing often disdain to take up posts as educational officials, while those who serve for a salary repeatedly neglect the work of teaching. Since the implementation of institutions depends upon people, might there still be ways to inspire and encourage them? In examining the reasons for the flourishing and decline, the rise and fall, of schools, talent, and government in ancient and modern times, one cannot avoid questions. I therefore put these matters to you students, hoping that you will trace their underlying causes and weigh what ought to be put into practice.

In antiquity, tribute was assessed according to the capacities of the soil. In the region of Yangzhou, the fields were rated lowest of the lowest. Today, the prefectures of the Wu area and the prefectures of Hu [?] all lie within the former territory of Yangzhou. Zhong Yong …

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
九曲吳夫差敗於欈李亦其處也今
其地號為都會田賦之供歲不下數百
萬石以天下論之大率十當八九而絲
纊布帛之屬取給民生日用者亦歲以
萬計夫地不大於古也民不加於昔也
而物產阜盛若此何以能致然也然其
間不幸而遇貪吏之侵漁豪強之兼并
天時之水旱不常有司之征徭不一侈
靡相師而浮費無節經界相侵而訟訐
===
不已負貸於公私者無完期掊克於上
下者無休曰以地產有限之利而欲給
公家無窮之用雖使尺寸而取之錙銖
而較之亦有不勝其弊者矣茲欲上下
恒足不病於國不困於民所以區處之
法何在古者諸侯之國其地可以出兵車
千乘今之山東河南諸郡即春秋齊魯
宋陳衛鄭諸國之地也考之當時自一

九曲吳，夫差敗於欈李，亦其處也。今其地號為都會，田賦之供歲不下數百萬石；以天下論之，大率十當八九。而絲纊布帛之屬，取給民生日用者，亦歲以萬計。夫地不大於古也，民不加於昔也，而物產阜盛若此，何以能致然也？然其間不幸而遇貪吏之侵漁、豪強之兼并、天時之水旱不常、有司之征徭不一，侈靡相師而浮費無節，經界相侵而訟訐不已，負貸於公私者無完期，掊克於上下者無休曰。以地產有限之利，而欲給公家無窮之用，雖使尺寸而取之、錙銖而較之，亦有不勝其弊者矣。茲欲上下恒足，不病於國，不困於民，所以區處之法何在？

古者諸侯之國，其地可以出兵車千乘。今之山東、河南諸郡，即春秋齊、魯、宋、陳、衛、鄭諸國之地也。考之當時，自一國宮室、官吏百需之外，如朝聘、會盟、征
translation_en:
… “nine bends,” Wu [?]; it was also here that Fuchai was defeated at Zuili. Today this region is renowned as a metropolitan center. Its annual land-tax contribution amounts to no fewer than several million shi of grain; reckoned against the total for the realm, it accounts for roughly eight or nine tenths. Silk, silk floss, cloth, and other textiles supplied for the people’s daily needs are likewise counted annually in tens of thousands. The land is no more extensive than in antiquity, nor is the population greater than formerly. How, then, has such abundance of products been achieved? Yet the region unfortunately suffers from the depredations of corrupt officials, the engrossment of land by powerful families, unpredictable floods and droughts, and inconsistent tax and labor demands by the responsible authorities. People emulate one another in extravagance, and needless expenditure knows no restraint. Encroachments upon field boundaries produce unending lawsuits and accusations. Those indebted to public and private lenders never reach the day of repayment, while exactions at higher and lower levels never cease [?]. With the limited yield of the land, they seek to meet the government’s limitless expenditure. Even if they exacted revenue from every inch of land and reckoned every tiny amount, the resulting harm would still be unbearable. If we now wish those above and below to enjoy constant sufficiency, without distress to the state or hardship to the people, what measures should be adopted?

In antiquity, the territories of the feudal lords could each furnish a thousand war chariots. The present prefectures of Shandong and Henan occupy the territories of the Spring and Autumn states of Qi, Lu, Song, Chen, Wei, and Zheng. Examining conditions at that time, beyond the myriad requirements of each state’s palaces, officials, and subordinate personnel, there were such matters as court visits and diplomatic missions, assemblies and covenants, and military expeditions…

□□□□□日，軍旅之調發、芻粟之轉輸，何以給之也？今也號為大藩，其民陶於聖化，安養休息已百餘年，無若昔之驅作之勞、攻戰之苦矣。然營伍多孱弱之丁，行陣乏勇敢之士，一遇邊警，則荷戈禦侮，而常不足於兵；野多閒曠之地，民多游惰之夫，一遇歲侵，則發廩賑饑，而常不足於食。夫同此地也，均此民也，在季世則有國富兵強之效，在治世則有民貧財匱之憂，何也？茲欲兵食恒給，常使其有餘，不使其不足，所以變通之要何先？諸生皆抱經濟而来，天下之事展轉於心素矣，其為我言之，以少裨廟堂之末議。
問：天下之事夥矣，姑舉其大而要者，與諸士子商之。府衛將校，所以典兵也。今貂蟬皆世其官，節鉞率安其土，雖干憲典而蔭襲自如，雖誤軍機而職任無改。又将□□或起於虛冒之功，故典兵
translation_en:
…[five illegible characters] days [?]—how were the mobilization of troops and the transport of fodder and grain provided for? Today these regions are called great provinces. Their people, nurtured by the sage emperor’s civilizing influence, have lived in peace and recuperated for more than a hundred years, free from the toil of forced labor and the suffering of warfare experienced in former times. Yet the military units contain many weak men, and the ranks lack brave soldiers. Whenever an alarm arises on the frontier and men must shoulder weapons to resist aggression, troops are always insufficient. Much land lies idle and uncultivated, and many people lead idle lives. Whenever a poor harvest occurs and the granaries are opened to relieve hunger, food is always insufficient. The land is the same, and the people are alike: why, then, did an age of decline achieve wealthy states and strong armies, while an age of good government faces the worry of impoverished people and depleted resources? If we now wish to ensure a constant supply of troops and provisions, always maintaining a surplus and preventing shortages, what should take priority among the essential reforms? You candidates have all come equipped with learning in statecraft and have long turned the affairs of the realm over in your minds. Explain your views to me, so that they may contribute something to the deliberations at court.
Question: The affairs of the realm are numerous. Let us select the most important and essential matters for discussion with you candidates. The commanders and officers of the military commissions and guards are charged with commanding troops. Today those who wear sable tails and cicada ornaments all hold their offices hereditarily, while those entrusted with the insignia of military command generally remain comfortably in their own territories. Even when they violate the laws, succession through hereditary privilege proceeds as usual; even when they mishandle military affairs, their appointments remain unchanged. Moreover, commanders [two illegible characters] [?] sometimes rise through falsely claimed military achievements. Thus those who command troops…

倖而苟安以養寇何以得將皆勇智而

punctuated:
者多挾負閥閲而肆惡以虐軍，怙恃恩倖而苟安以養寇。何以得將皆勇智，而兵不惰、寇不侵乎？

藩臬守令所以治民也。今藩臬入爲公卿，令長名居臺省，或一歲甫周而屢遷，或一考方稱而輒起。又况黜陟之典，或出於毁譽之私。故牧民者忽於撫字而承順以趨名，必於超遷而刻削以足欲。何以使吏皆廉靜，而事不煩、民不擾乎？

賦斂所以足國用也。往者吳楚諸郡倉廩皆充，農沾折銀之惠。今絲縷布帛亦征以粟，而官糴之法復行於市，其弊不可勝言者。何以使田野獲安，而且革其出納之弊乎？

漕運所以供京儲也。往者齊魯諸水舟楫易通，兵免殷剥之患。今支兌轉輸旣盡其力，而私債之息每償於人，其害不可勝言者。何以使河道無壅，而得去其稱貸之害乎？請詳陳之，期於必行，毋徒效書生之常談焉也。
translation_en:
…those commanding troops often rely on their distinguished family pedigrees to commit outrages and abuse their soldiers; trusting in favor and patronage, they seek their own ease and allow bandits to flourish. How can we ensure that all commanders are brave and wise, that soldiers are not idle, and that bandits do not invade?

Provincial administration commissioners and surveillance commissioners, prefects, and magistrates are charged with governing the people. Today, provincial commissioners enter the central government as high dignitaries, while magistrates gain appointments in the censorial and central administrative offices. Some receive repeated promotions when barely a year has passed; others are immediately advanced upon receiving a favorable rating in a single performance evaluation. Moreover, decisions on demotion and promotion sometimes arise from self-interested slander or praise. Thus those who shepherd the people neglect their care, seeking reputation through compliant deference to superiors; intent on exceptional promotion, they exact harsh levies to satisfy their desires. How can we ensure that officials are all incorruptible and restrained, that administration is not burdensome, and that the people are not harassed?

Taxes and levies provide for the state's expenses. Formerly, the granaries of the prefectures of Wu and Chu were all full, and farmers enjoyed the benefit of commuting their payments to silver. Now even levies in silk thread, cloth, and silk fabric are collected in grain, and official grain purchasing has again been introduced in the markets. The resulting abuses are too numerous to recount. How can we secure peace for the farming population and also eliminate abuses in the receipt and disbursement of these revenues?

Grain transport supplies the capital's reserves. Formerly, boats passed easily along the waterways of Qi and Lu, and soldiers were spared the scourge of heavy exactions. Now receiving and exchanging grain and transporting it onward exhaust their strength, while they must repeatedly pay interest to others on private debts. The resulting harms are too numerous to recount. How can we keep the waterways unobstructed and eliminate the harm caused by their borrowing? Please set forth your proposals in detail, with a view to their actual implementation; do not merely repeat the stock discussions of bookish scholars.

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
出門如見大賓使民如承大祭
趙寬
同考試官員外郎陳批此篇詞老而豐
理明而順本房之所無者錄之以式後學
同考試官編修王批詞不贅而意自足
同考試官編修商批場中作者率於大
賓大祭處牽強屬對殊為可厭是篇詞簡理明
宜用錄出
===
同考試官脩撰吳批題意易識此篇獨
愛其詞之整潔也取之
考試官學士王批行文暢達

text:
力乎盖凡人之情身焉出門以其至近至常由
也多有怠忽之者若夫見賓則其心愓然而敬
矣况所見者大賓乎賓之大敬之大也故出門
雖無大賓之是見宛若揖讓于擯介之間而不
愆于儀敬之存於出門者盖如此凡人之情事
焉使民以其至愚而易役也多有慢易之者若
夫承祭則其心肅然而敬矣况所承者大祭乎
祭之大敬之大也故使民雖無大祭之是承儼
若對越于郊廟之上而毋貳爾心敬之存於使

物則仁之用行為仁之道不外乎此二者是宜

translation_en:
…exert effort? In ordinary human feeling, going out of doors is so immediate and commonplace [?] that people often become careless and inattentive about it. When receiving a guest, however, their hearts become alert and reverent—how much more so when the guest is distinguished! The greater the guest’s standing, the greater the reverence. Thus, even when going out without a distinguished guest to receive, one should act as though bowing and yielding precedence among ceremonial ushers and attendants, committing no breach of propriety. Such is the preservation of reverence when going out of doors. In ordinary human feeling, when employing the common people, people often treat them with arrogance and contempt because they regard them as exceedingly ignorant and easy to put to work. When conducting a sacrifice, however, their hearts become solemn and reverent—how much more so when the sacrifice is a great one! The greater the sacrifice, the greater the reverence. Thus, even when employing the people without a great sacrifice to conduct, one should be as solemn as though standing before the spirits at the suburban altars or in the ancestral temple, allowing no division in one’s attention. Such is the preservation of reverence when employing the people.

When one goes out with reverence, the heart is gathered inward and selfish intentions naturally dissolve: benevolence is present at the time of going out. When one employs the people with reverence, the heart is held in restraint and selfish intentions naturally disappear: benevolence is present at the time of employing the people. Yet these are merely examples of going out and employing the people used to illustrate reverence. Extending this principle, where could one go that did not call for reverence? To discuss it further: through reverence one maintains oneself, and thus the substance of benevolence is established; through reciprocity one reaches out to others, and thus the operation of benevolence is realized. The way of practicing benevolence does not go beyond these two things. It was therefore fitting that the Master should present both together in instructing Zhonggong, and also have him examine their effects for himself. On another occasion Zhonggong said, “To abide in reverence and act with simplicity, and thereby govern the people.” Abiding in reverence means maintaining oneself through reverence; acting with simplicity means reaching out to others through reciprocity. Viewed in this light, his request to put into practice…

…one still does not know which constitutes excess, which falls short, and which is the mean. Shun comprehensively gathered the multitude of divergent opinions, grasping the furthest extremes of their differences. He weighed and measured them against the inherent standard, seeking what was most fitting in moral principle. Only then could he recognize that excess and deficiency lay on that side, among things that must not be put into practice, while what neither exceeded nor fell short lay on this side, among things that assuredly could be put into practice. Thereupon he applied it to the people. I see that his choosing was no mere choosing: everything he put into daily practice embodied this mean, without the slightest partiality or deviation. His scrutiny was no mere scrutiny: everything manifested in his undertakings and actions [?] embodied this mean, without the tiniest error. Even if he obtained it from grass-cutters and wood-gatherers, the mean found among them was his own mean; even if he obtained it from the common people, the mean found among them was his own mean.

Ah! Since Shun adopted what was good in this way, his choosing was supremely discerning and his practice supremely thorough. Is this not why his understanding neither exceeded nor fell short, and why the Way was put into practice? Moreover, from his farming, pottery-making, and fishing to his becoming emperor, Shun invariably learned from others. Could anyone have surpassed Shun in perceptiveness and intelligence? Yet he was so unwilling to rely solely on his own judgment. This is why, already a sage, he became ever more sagely. As for what is called grasping the two extremes and applying the mean, this is also the method of the mind transmitted by the sages. Consider what he received from Yao: “Truly hold fast to that mean.” When he transmitted it to Yu, he said: “Be discerning, be single-minded; truly hold fast to that mean.” Sage succeeded sage in this transmission; beyond the mean, no further profundity remained. Those who bear responsibility for putting the Way into practice must devote themselves to adopting what is good in others and applying the mean found in others; then…

text:
於衆人衆人之心豈能識乎君子獨不觀諸孔
子之事乎方孔子之仕於魯也桓子受女樂之
饋吾道已見沮於齊矣於此而不去邪則失夫
去就之宜而見幾非明决矣苟於此而遂行邪
則顯其君相之失而用意非忠厚矣故行不遂
行必待不致膰而後行去不苟去必俟其微罪
而後去使君相之失既泯於無迹而在己之行
又托於有故其見幾之明决既如彼而用意之

translation_en:
…from ordinary people. How could ordinary people, with their way of thinking, understand a gentleman? Have you not considered the case of Kongzi? When Kongzi was serving in Lu, Huanzi accepted a gift of female musicians, and the Way he upheld had already been obstructed by Qi. If he did not leave at this point, he would fail to act appropriately in leaving or remaining, and his discernment of the first signs of change would lack clarity and resolution. Yet if he departed immediately, he would expose the faults of his ruler and chief minister, and his intentions would lack loyalty and generosity. Thus, though he would depart, he did not depart immediately: he waited until the sacrificial meat was not sent to him before leaving. Nor did he leave heedlessly: he waited for a minor fault on their part before departing. In this way, the faults of the ruler and chief minister would disappear without a trace, while his own departure would have a reason to which it could be attributed. His clarity and resolution in discerning the first signs of change were such, and his loyalty and generosity of intention were likewise such. How could ordinary people understand this? Thus, those at the time who did not understand thought he had left over the meat; those who understood thought he had left over a breach of ritual propriety. Those who thought it was over the meat were certainly viewing the sage through their own selfish minds; who among them could know the subtle intention behind his leaving or staying? Those who thought it was over a breach of ritual propriety were measuring the sage by their shallow understanding; who among them could discern the profound intention behind his delaying or hastening his departure? If Kongzi’s mind lay beyond ordinary people’s understanding in this way, how could Mengzi’s mind have been understood by Kun?

In general, Kongzi in Lu and Mengzi in Qi initially took office with their resolve fixed upon the Way, and ultimately departed for a purpose. Their intentions were one and the same. To depart slowly, spending three nights before leaving Zhou, was indeed beyond others’ understanding, and something he himself found difficult to explain openly. Therefore, in response to Chunyu Kun’s criticism, Mengzi merely cited the case of Kongzi…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
无咎吾夫子引而釋之意謂人之常情相入則
相隨相拒則不隨故隨之為道不難於致亨而
艱於得正不重於大亨而重於无咎是故已有
能隨之道而人有來隨之心則聲應氣求不戒
而以孚也此感彼應不疾而自速也其為亨也
不亦大乎然必已无違道之干而人非于宗之
吝然後內不見已而无反无側焉外不見人而
无偏无黨焉所謂咎者不亦免乎夫處隨盡善
如此則天下豈有不隨之者哉蓋天下之人不
===
同而所同者此心隨而得正則通天下之心矣
天下之心不同而所同者此理隨而得正則得
天下之理矣吾見暘谷以西昧谷以東疆域雖
有彼此也而雲合嚮應者有異域而无異心焉
明都以北幽都以南地里雖有遠近也而輻輳
鱗集者有異地而无異志焉所隨得其正而天
下隨之則元亨不假言矣隨之道其大矣哉大
抵大其心然後能體天下之物公天下以為心
然後能一天下之心隨得其正大也公也天下

punctuated: 无咎。吾夫子引而釋之，意謂人之常情，相入則相隨，相拒則不隨。故隨之為道，不難於致亨而艱於得正，不重於大亨而重於无咎。是故已有能隨之道，而人有來隨之心，則聲應氣求，不戒而以孚也；此感彼應，不疾而自速也。其為亨也，不亦大乎？然必已无違道之干，而人非于宗之吝，然後內不見已，而无反无側焉；外不見人，而无偏无黨焉。所謂咎者，不亦免乎？夫處隨盡善如此，則天下豈有不隨之者哉？蓋天下之人不同，而所同者此心；隨而得正，則通天下之心矣。天下之心不同，而所同者此理；隨而得正，則得天下之理矣。吾見暘谷以西、昧谷以東，疆域雖有彼此也，而雲合嚮應者，有異域而无異心焉；明都以北、幽都以南，地里雖有遠近也，而輻輳鱗集者，有異地而无異志焉。所隨得其正，而天下隨之，則元亨不假言矣。隨之道，其大矣哉！大抵大其心，然後能體天下之物；公天下以為心，然後能一天下之心。隨得其正，大也，公也，天下
translation_en: …without blame. Our Master quoted these words and explained them. His meaning was that, in ordinary human feeling, mutual acceptance leads to mutual following, whereas mutual rejection prevents it. Thus, in the Way of Following, achieving success is not difficult; attaining correctness is difficult. What matters most is not great success but freedom from blame. Accordingly, when one possesses the Way by which others can follow, and others have the desire to come and follow, like sounds respond and like vital energies seek one another: trust arises without admonition. A stimulus here meets a response there: things hasten of themselves without being hurried. Is this not great success? Yet one must oneself commit no transgression against the Way [?], and others must be free of the narrowness of attachment to their own clan. Only then does one inwardly lose sight of oneself, without deviation or inclination to either side, and outwardly lose sight of distinctions among others, without partiality or faction. Is not what is called blame thereby avoided? If one thus achieves complete goodness in dealing with Following, how could anyone under Heaven fail to follow? For the people under Heaven differ, but what they share is this heart. When following attains correctness, one is in communion with the hearts of all under Heaven. The hearts of those under Heaven differ, but what they share is this principle. When following attains correctness, one grasps the principle shared by all under Heaven. I see that west of Yanggu and east of Meigu, although territories are distinct, those who gather like clouds and respond like echoes come from different regions but have no differences of heart. North of Mingdu and south of Youdu, although places differ in distance, those who converge like spokes at a hub and gather like closely arrayed scales come from different places but have no differences of purpose. When what is followed is correct and all under Heaven follow it, supreme success needs no further mention. How great is the Way of Following! In general, only by enlarging one's heart can one comprehend the things of the world; only by taking impartial concern for all under Heaven as one's heart can one unite the hearts of all under Heaven. Following that attains correctness is magnanimous and impartial; all under Heaven…

Examiner, Academician Xu, comments: “Making Heaven’s favor the basis of the argument is most apt.”

The great minister recounts the actual manifestations of Heaven’s favor and mandate, revealing the effects of the former kings’ assiduous cultivation of virtue. Virtue is the foundation for winning Heaven’s support. Heaven favored the former kings and brought their transformative governance to its highest flourishing: could this have resulted from anything other than their assiduous cultivation of virtue? Formerly, when Yi Yin instructed Tai Jia, he began by recounting the affairs of the Xia. He told him that when the earlier Xia rulers assiduously cultivated virtue, Heaven’s favor and mandate did far more than merely keep them free of calamities. Within their territorial boundaries, mountains stood and rivers flowed: the mountains suffered no diminution and the rivers never ran dry, each remaining secure in its place. Within the sphere of their sacrifices, the spirits in their hidden depths enjoyed the offerings and came into their presence, their numinous powers at rest. Yet this was not because mountains, rivers, and spirits became tranquil of themselves. It was simply that the rulers cultivated virtue assiduously, and Heaven favored them with its mandate.

Nor was this confined to the tranquility of mountains, rivers, and spirits. Birds and beasts, the feathered and furred kinds, are creatures that gather in groups. All moved briskly and freely [?], fulfilling their natures in flying and running. Fish and turtles, the scaled and shelled kinds, are creatures that stir with life. All swam actively and at ease, fulfilling their innate disposition to swim. Yet this was not because birds, beasts, fish, and turtles attained ease of themselves. It was simply that the rulers cultivated virtue assiduously, and Heaven favored them with its mandate. When the effects of cultivating virtue reached this extent, it goes without saying that the people’s lives at that time were secure and fulfilled.

There is no other reason for this: the ruler is lord of Heaven, Earth, spirits, and all things, and his virtue embodies the principle underlying Heaven, Earth, spirits, and all things. Thus Yi Yin insisted on speaking of Heaven and the Xia because Heaven is what a ruler must fear, and antiquity is the mirror in which he must examine himself. By fearing Heaven, he understands the source of disaster and blessing; by taking antiquity as his mirror, he understands where good and evil lie. Understanding brings apprehension; apprehension leaves him no leisure to rest at ease, and so he diligently cultivates virtue. Tai Jia heard these words and was able to maintain his virtue to the end, becoming an excellent ruler of the Shang. Great indeed was the efficacy of Yi Yin’s admonitions.
“Let him say: ‘I have received Heaven’s Mandate. May I fully match the years of the Xia and not fall short of the years of the Yin.’”

考試官學士徐批：善鋪叙題意。

期當代之受命，兼前代之永命，此大臣為賢王告也。盖受命之永，莫夏商若也。大臣欲君臣期受天命而兼之，忠愛之心何如哉！昔洛邑既成，召公作誥，托周公陳戒成王，及此謂夫君臣上下相與勤恤者，正欲期天命之永爾。是故克成厥勳，以撫方夏，文王膺天命於造周之時；祇承上帝，以遏亂畧，武王受天命於伐商之日。其得之於前人也既非一朝，則衍之於後人也豈特再世？彼前乎殷而有天下者，夏也。夏之歷年四百，可謂永矣。惟我有周，自服土中，丕若有夏之歷年，常使其命維新焉。後乎夏而有天下者，殷也。殷之歷年六百，可謂久矣。惟我有周，自時中乂，式勿替有殷之歷年，常使多方誕受焉。穆穆皇皇，胤祚何多也！皆得以保民於無窮，不惟同乎夏，而殷又足兼之矣。蟄蟄繩繩，嗣續何盛也！
translation_en:
…his loyal and loving heart overflows beyond the words of the composition.

Examiner Academician Wang comments: The meaning of aspiring to combine the enduring mandates is developed very aptly.

Examiner Academician Xu comments: Skillfully elaborates the meaning of the topic.

To aspire for the present dynasty’s receipt of the Mandate to encompass the enduring mandates of former dynasties: this is the admonition of a great minister to a worthy king. For the endurance of their mandates, none could equal Xia and Shang. The great minister wished ruler and ministers to aspire to receive Heaven’s Mandate and encompass the duration of both: how profound was his loyal devotion! Formerly, when Luoyi had been completed, the Duke of Shao composed his Announcement, entrusting the Duke of Zhou with conveying admonitions to King Cheng. When he reached this point, he explained that ruler and ministers, those above and those below, should together labor diligently and take anxious care precisely because they aspired to make Heaven’s Mandate endure. Thus, King Wen accomplished his great work and pacified the lands of Xia, receiving Heaven’s Mandate when he founded Zhou; King Wu reverently served the Lord on High and checked disorder and aggression, receiving Heaven’s Mandate when he attacked Shang. Since its acquisition by their predecessors was not the work of a single day, how could its extension to their descendants be limited to merely two generations?

The dynasty that possessed All under Heaven before Yin was Xia. Xia lasted four hundred years: this may indeed be called enduring. May our Zhou, having established its rule in the central land, grandly match the years of Xia, constantly keeping its Mandate renewed. The dynasty that possessed All under Heaven after Xia was Yin. Yin lasted six hundred years: this may indeed be called long-lasting. May our Zhou, governing from this central region, never fall short of the years of Yin, constantly enabling the many regions to receive its blessings in abundance. Solemn and resplendent—how abundant the blessings bestowed upon its descendants! All will be able to protect the people without end; Zhou will not merely equal Xia, but will also be able to encompass the duration of Yin. Multitudinous and unbroken—how flourishing the succession of descendants! …

translation_en:
…all may preside over the ancestral vessels with their position unshakable. Having already equaled Yin, they can also surpass Xia. If so, their reception of Heaven’s Mandate, traced back to Xia and Yin, will prove still more glorious; the transmission of their royal enterprise, measured against Kings Wen and Wu, will occasion no shame. Is this not what ruler and ministers should unitedly hope for? Alas! Heaven’s Mandate cannot simply be received without effort, nor can the royal enterprise be transmitted by good fortune alone. Human effort must necessarily play its part. Thus the Duke of Shao said, “Let those above and below diligently care for the people.” He also said, “I wish the king, through the common people, to receive Heaven’s enduring Mandate.” For attending to the common people gives substance to diligent care; receiving Heaven’s enduring Mandate gives substance to the length of the dynasty’s years. As for urgently revering virtue, this too must be pursued as the means of giving substance to sincerity toward the common people [?]. Ah! Only through such conduct can the Duke of Shao’s loyal and loving intentions be fulfilled!

…with teams of four stallions, arriving in an unbroken stream outside the palace walls, their harness bells ringing out resoundingly. At such a time, how could I continue sleeping peacefully instead of rising early to hold court? The many lords come for an audience, riding their ceremonial carriages in a continuous procession along the road to court; the jingling of their bells can be heard far away. At such a time, how could I remain at ease instead of rising at dawn to attend to government? Ah! Though dwelling within the palace, his thoughts are at work in the court: how supremely diligent the king of Zhou was in governing! In general, it is through unceasing diligence that the Way of Heaven brings all things to completion; it is through diligence that the Way of the ruler orders the myriad affairs of state. Since antiquity, emperors and kings have certainly made diligence in government their foundation, yet they have also invariably relied upon worthy consorts for assistance. Commentators say that King Xuan accepted Queen Jiang’s remonstrance and thereafter held court early and adjourned late, and that this poem was composed on that occasion. Ah! The poem asking “How goes the night?” and the historical account of her awaiting punishment in the palace’s secluded alley surely deserve to be handed down together as instruction for all generations!

“A mandate came from Heaven, charging this King Wen. In Zhou, in the capital, the woman who would continue your line came from Shen. Its eldest daughter went to you in marriage and gave birth to the great King Wu.”
Guo Wei

This essay excels in both expression and reasoning; therefore it has been selected for inclusion.

translation_en:
…The argument is upright and grand, and the language and tone gentle and refined: this composition achieves these qualities.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Expositor-in-Waiting: He understands the intent to place the principal emphasis on King Wu, and his language is also rich and ample. Commendable.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Expositor-in-Waiting: He describes the atmosphere of the Zhou house’s rise to kingship so vividly that it seems before our eyes. This should be recorded to show students of the Book of Odes.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician: He brings out how Heaven’s mandate bestowed abundant favor upon King Wu, while necessarily tracing its origins back to King Wen. This is precisely the meaning of the ode.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Academician: Gentle, refined, and appropriate in style.

When Heaven favors a sage by providing him with a sagely consort, it must further enrich its favor by bringing forth a sagely heir. For the birth of a sagely heir is what enables a dynasty’s royal enterprise to reach fulfillment. Having favored the sage by providing him with a sagely consort, how could Heaven fail to enrich its favor by bringing forth a sagely heir?

Formerly, when the Duke of Zhou admonished King Cheng, he intended to speak of King Wu’s campaign against Shang and therefore traced the matter to its origins. It was as though he said: People know only that our Zhou’s royal enterprise was completed under King Wu; they do not know that it actually originated with King Wen. Thus, great indeed is Heaven’s mandate! Issuing from beyond the azure heavens, it does not readily come to rest upon anyone. Yet now it had charged our King Wen in Zhou’s capital, and the force of the rise to kingship surged forth irresistibly. Heaven’s mandate operates amid the unseen and is not readily fathomed. Yet now it had charged our King Wen in Zhou’s capital, and the grand design for establishing the state shone forth, renewed. Such was Heaven’s favor toward our King Wen; thus it brought forth, in its abundant favor …

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
聖配於初載之際而克纘太任之女事者維此
莘國以其長子来嫁于周焉黙定嘉偶於將婚
之期而能嗣太任之徽音者維此大邦以其長
女曰嬪于京焉所以然者蓋以周德日新而王
業宜有所付商道寢衰而曆數宜有所歸故既
生文王以啓大勳矣又必篤之不已使復生武
王于以丕承厥志而大勳由之以集既生文王
以肇大統矣又必厚之不替使復生武王于以
克光前烈而大統由之以定噫天命之眷眷於
===
周如此然則武王之伐商而革命也一順乎天
爾夫豈人力私智之所及哉抑論之陰剝而陽
必復其剝也有初晦極而明必生其明也以漸
商之亡雖在於辛受之力行無度而積衰之勢
已兆於祖甲之怠荒周之王雖在於武王之燮
伐大商而方興之勢已原於太王之肇迹况夫
辛受而上帝乙武乙世縱其欲太王而下王季
文王世修其德天命之去留國祚之興廢豈一
朝一夕之故哉此周公戒成王之深意後之君

punctuated: 聖配於初載之際，而克纘太任之女事者，維此莘國以其長子来嫁于周焉。黙定嘉偶於將婚之期，而能嗣太任之徽音者，維此大邦以其長女曰嬪于京焉。所以然者，蓋以周德日新，而王業宜有所付；商道寢衰，而曆數宜有所歸。故既生文王以啓大勳矣，又必篤之不已，使復生武王，于以丕承厥志，而大勳由之以集；既生文王以肇大統矣，又必厚之不替，使復生武王，于以克光前烈，而大統由之以定。噫！天命之眷眷於周如此，然則武王之伐商而革命也，一順乎天爾，夫豈人力私智之所及哉？抑論之，陰剝而陽必復，其剝也有初；晦極而明必生，其明也以漸。商之亡，雖在於辛受之力行無度，而積衰之勢已兆於祖甲之怠荒；周之王，雖在於武王之燮伐大商，而方興之勢已原於太王之肇迹。况夫辛受而上，帝乙、武乙世縱其欲；太王而下，王季、文王世修其德。天命之去留，國祚之興廢，豈一朝一夕之故哉？此周公戒成王之深意，後之君
translation_en:
…a sage consort in those early years. The woman who could carry on Tai Ren’s womanly duties was the eldest daughter whom the state of Shen sent to marry into Zhou. Heaven silently determined a fitting match as the time for marriage approached: the woman who could inherit Tai Ren’s virtuous renown was the eldest daughter of this great state, who became a bride in the capital. This was because Zhou’s virtue was renewed daily, and the royal enterprise needed someone to whom it could be entrusted; Shang’s Way was steadily declining, and the allotted succession of sovereignty needed somewhere to devolve. Thus, having brought forth King Wen to initiate the great achievement, Heaven necessarily continued its generous favor without cease, causing King Wu in turn to be born, so that he might grandly carry on King Wen’s aspirations and thereby bring that achievement to completion. Having brought forth King Wen to inaugurate the great succession, Heaven necessarily sustained its abundant favor without diminution, causing King Wu in turn to be born, so that he might glorify his predecessor’s accomplishments and thereby secure that succession. Ah! Such was Heaven’s enduring solicitude for Zhou. King Wu’s attack on Shang and his transfer of the Mandate were therefore entirely in accord with Heaven. How could human strength or private ingenuity have accomplished this?
To consider the matter further: when yin strips away yang, yang must return, yet that stripping away has its beginning; when darkness reaches its extreme, light must arise, yet its emergence is gradual. Although Shang’s downfall came through Xin Shou’s unrestrained conduct, the tendency toward accumulated decline had already manifested itself in Zu Jia’s indolence and neglect. Although Zhou’s attainment of kingship came through King Wu’s assault upon great Shang, the momentum of its rise had already originated in King Tai’s founding endeavors. Moreover, before Xin Shou, Di Yi and Wu Yi indulged their desires generation after generation; after King Tai, Wang Ji and King Wen cultivated their virtue generation after generation. Could the departure or retention of Heaven’s Mandate, and the rise or fall of a dynasty’s fortunes, be the work of a single morning or evening? This was the profound meaning of the Duke of Zhou’s admonition to King Cheng. Those who would later rule…

Spring and Autumn Annals

The feudal lords covenanted at Shouzhi. The Earl of Zheng fled home without joining the covenant. Fifth year of Duke Xi.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, and the Earl of Cao to attack Zheng; they besieged Xincheng. Sixth year of Duke Xi.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju to covenant at Jiantu. The Duke paid court at the king’s quarters. The Duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Chen, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, and representatives of Qin at Wen. The Heavenly King hunted at Heyang. The Duke paid court at the king’s quarters. The feudal lords then besieged Xu. Twenty-eighth year of Duke Xi.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Right Supervising Secretary: Among examination candidates writing on this topic, few fail to grasp its purport, but most fall short in developing their discussion of the two sieges. This essay alone reads as though its author had been present at the time and witnessed the events himself. He weighs praise and blame with unwavering certainty, and furthermore unifies the essay through the two concepts of righteousness and ritual propriety. This especially reveals outstanding discernment.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Senior Compiler: In its treatment of the sieges of Zheng and Xu, this essay succeeds in dispensing with stock expressions and thoroughly assimilating the meaning of the commentary into its exposition. Excellent!

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician: The argument is balanced and sound.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Academician: The principles governing the wording of the annals are treated with care and rigor.

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
伯主明義貳國棄之固可討伯主脩禮與國違
之尤可討此鄭逃首止之盟許背王所之朝桓
文圍其國以討之夫豈過耶何則元良之位人
心所共属也乃今惠王寵帶子鄭危疑是時齊
桓主伯憂于厥心故合同會世子之邦再申首
止寧周之約大本由是而定儲位由是而安桓
公斯舉義云著矣夫何鄭為王室懿親敢逃大
眾之盟下行匹夫之事是則鄭文之逃非逃齊
也逃翼戴之義也桓也容可以不討乎遂舉伐
===
鄭之師圍其新造之邑執言棄義以討不庭雖
曰伐國圍邑事非美也殊不知圍鄭之圍為王
儲計耳果可以此而廢桓之功耶若夫方嶽之
覲臣子所當脩也乃今襄王勞晉鑾輿下臨是
時晉文率眾奔問起居首朝于踐土罷盟之日
再朝于會温請狩之時述職之遺風未泯朝宗
之大義猶存文公是舉禮亦至矣夫何許距踐
土河陽為密邇當諸侯之再會獨一跡之不來
是則許僖之慢非慢晉也慢覲王之禮也文也

曰伐國圍邑事非美也殊不知圍鄭之圍爲王
儲計耳果可以此而廢桓之功耶若夫方嶽之

之大義猶存文公是舉禮亦至矣夫何許距踐

是則許僖之慢非慢晉也慢覲王之禮也文也
punctuated:
伯主明義，貳國棄之，固可討；伯主脩禮，與國違之，尤可討。此鄭逃首止之盟，許背王所之朝，桓、文圍其國以討之，夫豈過耶？何則？元良之位，人心所共属也。乃今惠王寵帶，子鄭危疑。是時齊桓主伯，憂于厥心，故合同會世子之邦，再申首止寧周之約。大本由是而定，儲位由是而安，桓公斯舉，義云著矣。夫何鄭為王室懿親，敢逃大眾之盟，下行匹夫之事？是則鄭文之逃，非逃齊也，逃翼戴之義也。桓也，容可以不討乎？遂舉伐鄭之師，圍其新造之邑，執言棄義，以討不庭。雖曰伐國圍邑，事非美也，殊不知圍鄭之圍，為王儲計耳。果可以此而廢桓之功耶？
若夫方嶽之覲，臣子所當脩也。乃今襄王勞晉，鑾輿下臨。是時晉文率眾奔問起居，首朝于踐土罷盟之日，再朝于會温請狩之時。述職之遺風未泯，朝宗之大義猶存，文公是舉，禮亦至矣。夫何許距踐土、河陽為密邇，當諸侯之再會，獨一跡之不來？是則許僖之慢，非慢晉也，慢覲王之禮也。文也，
translation_en:
When a hegemon makes righteousness manifest and a disloyal state abandons it, that state may certainly be punished. When a hegemon observes ritual propriety and an allied state violates it, that state is all the more deserving of punishment. Thus, when Zheng absented itself from the covenant at Shouzhi and Xu neglected the audience at the king’s whereabouts, Dukes Huan and Wen besieged their states to punish them. How could this have been excessive? Why is this so? The position of the heir apparent is what all people’s hearts acknowledge together. Yet King Hui favored Dai, and his son Zheng’s position became precarious and uncertain. At that time Duke Huan of Qi held the hegemony and was deeply concerned. He therefore assembled the states that had met with the heir apparent and reaffirmed the agreement at Shouzhi to secure the Zhou royal house. Through this, the great foundation was settled and the succession secured. In this undertaking, Duke Huan’s righteousness was manifest. Why, then, did Zheng, a close kinsman of the royal house, dare to evade the covenant of the assembled lords and stoop to acting like a private individual? Duke Wen of Zheng’s evasion was therefore not an evasion of Qi, but of the righteous duty to support and uphold the royal heir. Could Duke Huan possibly refrain from punishing him? He consequently raised an army against Zheng and besieged its newly built town, citing its abandonment of righteousness as grounds for punishing its failure to render homage. Although attacking a state and besieging a town may be called unworthy acts, this fails to recognize that the siege of Zheng was undertaken solely for the royal heir’s sake. Can this really justify denying Duke Huan’s achievement?
As for audiences with the king at the regional sacred mountains, these are observances that subjects ought to fulfill. Now King Xiang came down in his royal carriage to acknowledge Jin’s services. Duke Wen of Jin then led the assembled lords in hastening to inquire after the king’s well-being. They first attended court at Jiantu on the day the covenant proceedings concluded, and attended again when they assembled at Wen and requested a royal hunt. The surviving custom of reporting on their duties had not vanished, and the great principle of paying court to the sovereign still endured. In this undertaking, Duke Wen’s observance of ritual propriety was consummate. Why, then, when Xu was so close to Jiantu and Heyang, did its ruler alone fail to make any appearance at the lords’ second assembly? Duke Xi of Xu’s disrespect was therefore not disrespect toward Jin, but disrespect for the ritual duty of appearing before the king. As for Duke Wen, …

《春秋》始惡強夷虐貳，而美伯者安攘之有屬；終惡強夷虐貳，而美伯者安攘之尤勤。此可見楚再伐鄭，其勢益張；晉再救鄭，其謀益善。《春秋》得不託書法以寓意哉？且鄭自皇戍見執，已懷棄楚之心；垂棘有盟，遂堅從晉之約。當是時也，楚共即遣嬰齊率彼豺狼之衆，凌我懿親之邦，盖憤鄭人背己，又乘其喪而伐之。然不義雖甚，而勢猶未熾也。晉景於此，將何如其為謀耶？乃命欒書之上將，往解鄭國之倒懸。繞角一遇，而荊蠻之師退矣。未幾，移兵侵蔡，而桑隧之敵復來；不戰還師，而三卿之謀以定。此書之善，景之善也。外攘内安，其有所屬哉！故《春秋》書欒書救鄭

…not a single detail of the events, from beginning to end, is omitted. Moreover, his other essays are all of comparable merit. Such an achievement would scarcely be possible for anyone who had not devoted himself wholeheartedly to this Classic. It is fitting that he should be recommended for selection among the foremost candidates.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician: His treatment, grounded in the commentary, of bringing peace to the various Xia states and repelling the Yi and Di is highly commendable.
Comment by Examiner Xu, Academician: His discussion of Duke Jing of Jin’s pacification of the Xia states and repulsion of the outsiders accords closely with the meaning of the commentary.
The Spring and Autumn Annals initially condemns the powerful outsiders for oppressing those whose allegiance was divided, while praising the hegemon for entrusting pacification and repulsion to a suitable man. In the later instance, it condemns the powerful outsiders for oppressing those whose allegiance was divided, while praising the hegemon for his still greater diligence in pacification and repulsion. Here we see that when Chu attacked Zheng a second time, its power grew still greater; when Jin rescued Zheng a second time, its plans grew still better. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to convey its meaning through its manner of recording these events? Now, ever since Huang Shu was taken prisoner, Zheng had harbored the intention of abandoning Chu. With the covenant at Chuiji, it firmly committed itself to following Jin. At this time, Duke Gong of Chu dispatched Yingqi to lead his wolfish host against our state of close royal kinship. Indignant that the people of Zheng had turned against him, he also took advantage of their mourning to attack them. Yet, although his injustice was extreme, his power had not yet reached its height. What plan, then, would Duke Jing of Jin devise? He ordered his chief commander, Luan Shu, to go and deliver Zheng from its desperate plight. After a single encounter at Raojiao, the army of the southern outsiders withdrew. Before long, Jin shifted its troops to invade Cai, and the enemy came against it again at Sangsui. Jin brought its army home without fighting, adopting the counsel of the three ministers. This was to Shu’s credit, and to Duke Jing’s credit as well. Repelling threats abroad and securing peace within had indeed been entrusted to the right man! Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records Luan Shu’s rescue of Zheng…

于嬰齊伐鄭之下者，所以美之也。罪楚之意，不於是而可見乎？曾幾何時，楚共復遣嬰齊督其師以越境，陳于氾以伐鄭，盖怒鄭之從晉，益肆其威以脅之。然爭衡猶舊，而勢則大張也。晉景於此，又何如其為援耶？乃合八國之君，躬赴鄭人之難。鍾儀一虜，而楚將之心寒矣。未幾，率此友邦，復講馬陵之信，同病荆楚，毋忘蟲牢之盟。此眾之志，景之志也。安夏攘夷，抑何其勤哉！故《春秋》書救鄭，書同盟于嬰齊再伐之下者，所以予之也。甚楚之橫，不於是而益彰乎？吁！楚數病鄭，則鄭果於背楚也可知；晉屢恤鄭，則鄭堅於從晉也可見。出谷遷喬，善亦著矣。特惜夫楚人重賂一至，鄭伯初心潛移。不二三載，銅鞮之執、欒書之伐、黑背之侵、脩澤之盟，其國殆不可為也。雖然，晉德亦於是乎衰矣。彼從違無常之鄭，又何足道哉！

translation_en:
…after the entry recording Ying Qi’s attack on Zheng: this is to praise him. Is the intention to condemn Chu not apparent here? Before long, Duke Gong of Chu again dispatched Ying Qi to lead his army across the border and draw up his forces at Fan to attack Zheng. Angered by Zheng’s adherence to Jin, he unleashed still greater force to intimidate it. The contest for supremacy continued as before, but Chu’s power had now greatly expanded. How, then, did Duke Jing of Jin come to Zheng’s aid? He assembled the rulers of eight states and personally went to relieve the people of Zheng in their distress. Once Zhong Yi had been taken prisoner, the Chu commanders lost heart. Soon afterward, he led these friendly states in renewing their pledges at Maling: all shared their grievance against Jing-Chu and were not to forget the covenant at Chonglao. This was the resolve of them all, and it was Duke Jing’s resolve. How diligently he worked to secure the Xia states and repel the outsiders! Thus, when the Spring and Autumn Annals records the rescue of Zheng and the joint covenant after Ying Qi’s second attack, it does so to express approval. Does the enormity of Chu’s aggression not thereby become still more evident?

Alas! From Chu’s repeated oppression of Zheng, we can understand Zheng’s determination to turn against Chu; from Jin’s repeated solicitude for Zheng, we can see Zheng’s steadfastness in adhering to Jin. Like a bird leaving a valley to settle in a lofty tree, Zheng had clearly shown its turn toward the good. It is only regrettable that, as soon as rich bribes arrived from Chu, the Earl of Zheng’s original intentions quietly shifted. Within two or three years came the detention at Tongdi, Luan Shu’s attack, Hei Bei’s incursion, and the covenant at Xiuze: his state had become almost impossible to manage. Even so, Jin’s virtue, too, was declining at this time. As for Zheng, so inconstant in its allegiance and defiance, what more is there to say?

正樂隨地而流行善心隨人而感動夫感人之
深者莫如樂也今焉於行感動之無閒則先王
立樂之方何如哉且夫正樂之作也制為雅頌
之聲比之八音之器聲足樂而不流文足論而
不息曲直繁瘠廉肉節奏俾者不足以感動人
之善心乎是故宗廟之中有君臣上下也禮法
森嚴之地以敬為主人孰不有是敬心耶非僻
punctuated:
莫不和敬；在族長鄉里之中，長幼同聽之，則莫不和順；在閨門之内，父子兄弟同聽之，則莫不和親。
孫交。
同考試官署員外郎林批：此作發明樂之感動善心，殆無餘蘊；末復體出和禮意，尤妙。
同考試官脩撰謝批：舂容平淡，正如雅頌之樂。
