正樂隨地而流行，善心隨人而感動。夫感人之深者，莫如樂也。今焉流行感動之無間，則先王立樂之方何如哉？且夫正樂之作也，制為雅頌之聲，比之八音之器，聲足樂而不流，文足論而不息。曲直、繁瘠、廉肉、節奏，何者不足以感動人之善心乎？是故宗廟之中，有君臣上下也。禮法森嚴之地，以敬為主，一人孰不有是敬心耶？非僻
translation_en:
…none fail to become harmonious and reverent. Among clan elders and in village communities, when old and young listen together, none fail to become harmonious and compliant. Within the household, when fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers listen together, none fail to become harmonious and affectionate.

Sun Jiao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Acting Vice Director: This composition elucidates how music stirs the goodness of the heart, leaving virtually nothing unexplored. Its conclusion further gives expression to the idea of harmonizing ritual, which is especially fine.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Compiler: Spacious and unhurried, plain and mild—just like the music of the Odes and Hymns.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician: It explains how music can stir human hearts into harmony; its language and tone are dignified and composed.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Academician: Expressive and penetrating.

Correct music spreads wherever it is performed, and the goodness of the heart is stirred in everyone who hears it. Nothing moves people as profoundly as music. Now, if its circulation and its power to move admit of no interruption, what must have been the method by which the former kings established music?

When correct music was created, it was fashioned into the sounds of the Odes and Hymns and attuned to instruments of the eight materials. Its sounds suffice to delight without becoming unrestrained; its patterned expression provides inexhaustible matter for discussion [?]. Its winding and straight passages, its fullness and spareness, its sharpness and richness, its measured rhythms—which of these does not suffice to stir the goodness of the human heart?

Thus, within the ancestral temple there are rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors. In this setting of solemn ritual rules, reverence is paramount. Who does not possess this reverent heart? Deviant and perverse influences…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
干之斯不敬者有矣樂行而同聽焉則敬不徒
敬一和敬以相臨雖雖肅肅何有倍畔之敗乎
族長鄉里之中有長幼也生齒羣聚之也以順
為主人孰不有是順心耶邪僻雜之斯不順者
有矣樂行而同聽焉則順不徒順一和順以相
接怡怡秩秩何有爭鬭之獄乎至若閨門之內
有父子焉有兄弟焉是乃恩掩義之地豈不以
親愛為主耶是心也人皆有之亦或失之以放
僻耳樂行而同聽之則以孝以慈有相親而無
===
相亮以恭以友有相親而無相戕親不徒親而
已是其和親也又何如然則固宥之善必由樂
而後興自然之倫必由樂而後正此樂所以為
人情之所不能免歟抑又論之禮之與樂未嘗
不相須而為用故宗廟之敬族長鄉里之順閨
門之親皆禮之所以行君臣上下聽之而和敬
長幼聽之而和順父子兄弟聽之而和親又樂
之所以達禮之序非樂固不足以和之也噫禮
行矣而和之以樂樂作矣而節之以禮古之□

punctuated: 干之，斯不敬者有矣。樂行而同聽焉，則敬不徒敬，一和敬以相臨，雖雖肅肅，何有倍畔之敗乎？族長鄉里之中有長幼也，生齒羣聚之也，以順為主，人孰不有是順心耶？邪僻雜之，斯不順者有矣。樂行而同聽焉，則順不徒順，一和順以相接，怡怡秩秩，何有爭鬭之獄乎？至若閨門之內，有父子焉，有兄弟焉，是乃恩掩義之地，豈不以親愛為主耶？是心也，人皆有之，亦或失之以放僻耳。樂行而同聽之，則以孝以慈，有相親而無相亮；以恭以友，有相親而無相戕。親不徒親而已，是其和親也，又何如？然則固宥之善，必由樂而後興；自然之倫，必由樂而後正。此樂所以為人情之所不能免歟？抑又論之，禮之與樂，未嘗不相須而為用。故宗廟之敬、族長鄉里之順、閨門之親，皆禮之所以行；君臣上下聽之而和敬，長幼聽之而和順，父子兄弟聽之而和親，又樂之所以達。禮之序，非樂固不足以和之也。噫！禮行矣，而和之以樂；樂作矣，而節之以禮。古之□
translation_en:
…interfere with it, and thus some become disrespectful. When music is performed and they listen together, their reverence becomes more than reverence alone: all approach one another with harmonious reverence, solemn and dignified [?]. How could there be the ruin brought by disobedience and rebellion? Among clan elders and in village communities there are elders and juniors. These are places where people gather [?], and deference is paramount. Who does not possess this disposition toward deference? When perversity intrudes, some become insubordinate. When music is performed and they listen together, their deference becomes more than deference alone: all deal with one another in harmony and deference, amiably and in due order. How could there be lawsuits arising from quarrels and fights?

As for the household, there are fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers. This is a setting where affection overshadows righteousness: surely love and affection are paramount here? Everyone possesses this disposition, though some lose it through dissipation and perversity. When music is performed and they listen together, filial devotion and parental kindness bring mutual affection without mutual estrangement [?]; respect from younger brothers and kindness from elder brothers bring mutual affection without mutual injury. Their affection becomes more than affection alone. What, then, must their harmonious affection be like? Thus, inherent goodness [?] must be aroused through music, and natural human relationships must be set right through music. Is this why music is something human feelings cannot dispense with?

To consider the matter further, ritual and music have always depended upon one another in their operation. Thus reverence in the ancestral temple, deference among clan elders and in village communities, and affection within the household are all ways in which ritual is put into practice. When rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors, hear music and become harmonious in their reverence; when elders and juniors hear it and become harmonious in their deference; and when fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers, hear it and become harmonious in their affection—these, in turn, are what music brings to fulfillment. The order established by ritual cannot be harmonized without music. Ah! Once ritual is practiced, music brings harmony to it; once music is performed, ritual regulates it. In antiquity, the □ …

…the kingly Way was fully realized and orderly government of the people put into practice: surely there was a reason for this!

“Therefore the Son of Heaven personally ploughs in the southern suburbs to supply the grain for sacrificial offerings.”
By Xu Jian.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Acting Vice Director: The meaning of this passage of the classic is very clear. Students give it no attention; most merely guess at its meaning and cobble together borrowed material. This is the only essay I have seen that fully grasps the principle and expresses it effectively.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Senior Compiler: Those who discuss ritual nowadays often use narrow views and conjectures to search deeply for some governing idea, while giving no serious thought to the broad meaning of the classics and their commentaries. In a topic such as this, the classic’s meaning is perfectly clear. What further governing idea was there ever to seek? Yet they all lose their way in bewilderment. Here is proof of the harm caused by pursuing the branches and neglecting the root. This composition integrates its learning into a coherent understanding; it is detailed, orderly, refined, and precise. Might its author be someone who devotes attention to inner cultivation and does not chase the fashions of the day?

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician: Clear in principle and ample in expression.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Academician: It closely apprehends the classics and their commentaries and assimilates them into a finished essay. An excellent composition.

The ruler fully expresses his personal reverence and prepares the things needed for sacrifices to his ancestors. If the sacrificial grain is not ready, he dares not offer sacrifice. Thus, exalted though the Son of Heaven is, how could he fail to exert himself personally to prepare it? Such is the meaning of the passage in “The Principles of Sacrifice.” Now, the Son of Heaven is lord of his subjects and bears the weighty responsibility of maintaining the ancestral temple. When he sacrifices, all within the Four Seas come with the contributions required by their respective duties. What need has he to plough? Even if ploughing is necessary, it is not as though there were no one to exert himself on his behalf; moreover …

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
何事於親乎殊不知君子之祭觀其敬而時君
子之敬本乎內之盡內不有以盡其志外何足
以盡其物哉故必於國之南郊為藉千畝冕而
朱紘秉耒三推斯時也錐三公五推卿諸侯九
推而庶人助以終畝然致敬發情竭力從事以
一人為之率先是豈徒然也哉正以共宗廟之
齊盛耳彼黍稷曰齊在器曰盛春礿夏禘之時
秋嘗冬烝之日水草之菹陸產之醢雖備矣不
可無薌合之黍以共八簋之實昆蟲之異草木
===
之實雖備矣不可無明粢之稷以實八簋之薦
今也藉必親耕則夫御廩之所藏莫非是敬之
所寓礿禘之行於是乎取之而不匱嘗烝之行
於是乎用之而有餘矣夫耕必於南郊者以陽
莫盛於南而耕則陽之事耳祭獨言齊盛者以
物莫美於穀而黍稷又穀之美耳天子之所以
自致而備物者如此祭之道寧有不盡乎抑是
耕也豈惟以共宗廟之事而已哉以之事天地
者此也以之事山川事社稷者亦此也合而言

punctuated: 何事於親乎？殊不知君子之祭，觀其敬而時。君子之敬，本乎內之盡；內不有以盡其志，外何足以盡其物哉？故必於國之南郊為藉千畝，冕而朱紘，秉耒三推。斯時也，錐三公五推，卿諸侯九推，而庶人助以終畝，然致敬發情，竭力從事，以一人為之率先，是豈徒然也哉？正以共宗廟之齊盛耳。彼黍稷曰齊，在器曰盛。春礿夏禘之時，秋嘗冬烝之日，水草之菹、陸產之醢雖備矣，不可無薌合之黍，以共八簋之實；昆蟲之異、草木之實雖備矣，不可無明粢之稷，以實八簋之薦。今也藉必親耕，則夫御廩之所藏，莫非是敬之所寓。礿禘之行，於是乎取之而不匱；嘗烝之行，於是乎用之而有餘矣。夫耕必於南郊者，以陽莫盛於南，而耕則陽之事耳。祭獨言齊盛者，以物莫美於穀，而黍稷又穀之美耳。天子之所以自致而備物者如此，祭之道寧有不盡乎？抑是耕也，豈惟以共宗廟之事而已哉？以之事天地者，此也；以之事山川、事社稷者，亦此也。合而言
translation_en:
…why, then, must he do it in person? This overlooks the fact that, in a gentleman’s sacrifices, one observes his reverence and his observance of the proper seasons. A gentleman’s reverence rests upon the fullest commitment of his inner self. Unless he fully commits his intentions inwardly, how can he fully provide the offerings outwardly? Thus he must establish a sacrificial field of a thousand mu in the southern suburb of the capital and, wearing a ceremonial crown with crimson chin-cords, take up the plow and make three pushes. At this time, although [?] the Three Dukes make five pushes, the ministers and regional lords nine, and the common people assist in finishing the fields, it is the One Man—the sovereign—who leads them in expressing reverence, giving voice to their feelings, and exerting their utmost strength in the task. Could this possibly be an empty exercise? Its precise purpose is to supply the grain offerings for the ancestral temple. Millet and panicled millet are called zi; placed in vessels, they are called cheng.

At the spring yue and summer di sacrifices, and on the days of the autumn chang and winter zheng sacrifices, even when pickled aquatic plants and minced meats from land animals have been prepared, there must also be millet, ritually called “fragrant union,” to fill the eight gui vessels. Even when unusual insects and the fruits of plants and trees have been prepared, there must also be panicled millet, ritually called “bright grain,” to fill the offerings in the eight gui vessels. Since the sovereign must personally plow the sacrificial field, everything stored in the imperial granary embodies this reverence. When the yue and di sacrifices are performed, supplies are drawn from it without exhaustion; when the chang and zheng sacrifices are performed, its stores are used and still remain abundant.

Plowing must take place in the southern suburb because nowhere is yang more abundant than in the south, and plowing is an activity belonging to yang. In speaking of sacrifice, grain offerings alone are singled out because no produce is finer than grain, and millet and panicled millet are the finest grains. Such is the way the Son of Heaven personally devotes himself to preparing the offerings. How could the proper way of sacrifice fail to be fulfilled? Moreover, is this plowing solely to supply the services of the ancestral temple? What is used to serve Heaven and Earth comes from this; what is used to serve the mountains and rivers, and the altars of Soil and Grain, likewise comes from this. Taken together, then …

第貳塲

論

聖賢道在萬世

孫交

When the sage kings of antiquity offered sacrifices, the heavenly spirits descended, the earthly deities arrived, and the spirits of the departed enjoyed the offerings. text:
論曰斯道之傳於天地間其所自者遠矣
本於天命之性具於衆人之心而大備於
聖賢之身聖賢之於斯道也知之既明行
之亦至授受於當時而筆之於書以詔萬
世書在萬世則道在萬世矣使非筆之於
書則道自聖賢而明亦自聖賢而止道自
聖賢而行亦自聖賢而止欲道在萬世弗
可得已是則斯道之傳於天地間其所自

translation_en:
The discourse states: The transmission of this Way throughout Heaven and Earth has origins reaching far into the past. It is rooted in the nature conferred by Heaven, present in the hearts of all people, and fully embodied in the sages and worthies. The sages and worthies understood this Way clearly and practiced it to the utmost. They transmitted and received it in their own times and committed it to writing to instruct all succeeding ages. If the writings endure for all ages, then the Way endures for all ages. Had they not committed it to writing, the Way would have been made clear by the sages and worthies, but would also have ended with them; it would have been put into practice by the sages and worthies, but would likewise have ended with them. To wish that the Way should endure for all ages would then have been futile. Thus, indeed, the transmission of this Way throughout Heaven and Earth has origins reaching far into the past! Since the Way of the sages and worthies endures for all ages, their achievement benefits all ages. Surely it is fitting to honor their virtue and requite their achievements by offering them royal sacrifices forever!

The earlier Confucian master Zhu Xi, discussing why the sages and worthies ought to receive sacrifices and tracing the grounds for those sacrifices, said that their Way endures for all ages. Profound indeed is his meaning. Allow me to trace it to its source. Before the sages and worthies were born, this Way resided in Heaven and Earth; once they were born, it resided in them. What is the Way of the sages and worthies? In its substance, it is the nature comprising benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness. In its functioning, it is the feelings of compassion, shame and aversion, deference and yielding, and approval and disapproval. Its human relationships are those between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend. Its cultural expressions are the Book of Changes, the Book of Documents, the Book of Odes, the Spring and Autumn Annals, rites, and music. This Way is certainly something that all people can understand and practice. Yet the knowledgeable go too far in their understanding, and already regard …

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
道為不足行愚者不及知又不求所以行
賢者行之過既以道為不足知不肖者不
及行又不求所以知此其所以不明不行
耳惟夫聖人則生而知之安而行之所謂
自誠而明也賢人則學而知之勉而行之
所謂自明而誠也使其達而在上以其明
於心行於身者舉而措之天下則道行於
當時使其窮而在下與其徒著書立言以
明道於當時則道雖不得行於當時亦必
===
行於後世矣若伏羲神農黃帝堯舜禹湯
文武之為君臯夔稷契伊傅周召之為臣
此聖賢之達而得以明道行道為事者也
若孔子之為師顏曾之為徒惟明帝王之
道以傳於來世此聖賢之窮無行道之位
而以明道為事者也然其道之傳也以心
傳耶抑以言傳耶曰以心傳於當時而以
言傳於來世言之所傳者何六經是已觀
孔子之賛易自羲農而下則羲農以下之

孔子之贊易自羲農而下則羲農以下之
punctuated:
道為不足行，愚者不及知，又不求所以行；賢者行之過，既以道為不足知，不肖者不及行，又不求所以知。此其所以不明不行耳。惟夫聖人則生而知之，安而行之，所謂自誠而明也；賢人則學而知之，勉而行之，所謂自明而誠也。使其達而在上，以其明於心、行於身者，舉而措之天下，則道行於當時；使其窮而在下，與其徒著書立言，以明道於當時，則道雖不得行於當時，亦必行於後世矣。若伏羲、神農、黃帝、堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之為君，臯、夔、稷、契、伊、傅、周、召之為臣，此聖賢之達而得以明道行道為事者也。若孔子之為師，顏、曾之為徒，惟明帝王之道，以傳於來世，此聖賢之窮，無行道之位，而以明道為事者也。
然其道之傳也，以心傳耶？抑以言傳耶？曰：以心傳於當時，而以言傳於來世。言之所傳者何？六經是已。觀孔子之賛《易》，自羲農而下，則羲農以下之
translation_en:
…the Way as not worth putting into practice; the foolish fall short in understanding and do not seek the means of practicing it. The worthy go too far in their practice and regard the Way as not worth understanding; the unworthy fall short in practice and do not seek the means of understanding it. This is why the Way is neither understood nor practiced. Sages alone know it from birth and practice it with ease: this is what is meant by proceeding from sincerity to understanding. Worthy people know it through learning and practice it through effort: this is what is meant by proceeding from understanding to sincerity. If they attain prominence and occupy high positions, they apply throughout the realm what they understand in their hearts and practice in their own persons, and thus the Way is practiced in their time. If they remain without opportunity and occupy lowly positions, they write books and formulate teachings with their disciples to elucidate the Way in their time. Then, even if the Way cannot be practiced in their own time, it will surely be practiced in later generations. Such rulers as Fuxi, Shennong, Huangdi, Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and such ministers as Gao Yao, Kui, Hou Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, Zhou Gong, and Shao Gong, were sages and worthies who attained prominence and could devote themselves to elucidating and practicing the Way. Kongzi as teacher, and Yan Hui and Zeng Shen as disciples, devoted themselves solely to elucidating the Way of the emperors and kings so as to transmit it to future generations. These were sages and worthies who lacked opportunity and held no position from which to put the Way into practice, and therefore made elucidating it their task.
Yet was their Way transmitted through the heart, or through words? The answer is: through the heart to their contemporaries, and through words to future generations. What are the words through which it was transmitted? They are the Six Classics. Consider Kongzi’s elucidation of the Book of Changes, beginning with Fuxi and Shennong and proceeding onward: then the Way from Fuxi and Shennong onward…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
道載於易書曰自唐虞而下則唐虞以下
之道載於書刪詩自商周而下則商周之
道載於詩修春秋則始於魯隱定禮樂則
原於虞夏帝王之道本於春秋禮樂中載
乎是則六經書也其所載者道也書傳於
一世則道在一世矣書傳於十世則道在
十世矣又傳之至於百世千世萬世焉則
道又在百千萬世矣猶未可以世計也日
月焉常明此道與日月同常明也宇宙焉
===
常清此道與宇宙同常清也山川之流峙
草木之敷榮此道豈不與之同一流峙敷
榮之常哉推而極之天地無窮此道亦與
之相為無窮矣夫道在萬世則功在萬世
而萬世之學者誦其書傳其道被聖賢之
澤於萬世之下其心與聖賢之心相為脗
合其氣與聖賢之氣相為流通此萬世之
學者所以報而祀之無有終窮而後王崇
德報功之典亦有隆而無替也自古聖賢

道載於《易》。書曰自唐虞而下，則唐虞以下之道載於《書》；刪《詩》自商周而下，則商周之道載於《詩》；修《春秋》，則始於魯隱；定禮樂，則原於虞夏。帝王之道本於《春秋》禮樂中載乎？是則六經，書也；其所載者，道也。書傳於一世，則道在一世矣；書傳於十世，則道在十世矣；又傳之至於百世、千世、萬世焉，則道又在百千萬世矣。猶未可以世計也。日月焉常明，此道與日月同常明也；宇宙焉常清，此道與宇宙同常清也。山川之流峙，草木之敷榮，此道豈不與之同一流峙敷榮之常哉？推而極之，天地無窮，此道亦與之相為無窮矣。

translation_en:
…the Way is recorded in the Changes. As for the Documents, beginning with Tang Yao and Yu Shun [?], the Way from their time onward is recorded in the Documents. In expurgating the Odes, Confucius began with the Shang and Zhou, so the Way of the Shang and Zhou is recorded in the Odes. In compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals, he began with Duke Yin of Lu; in establishing rites and music, he traced their origins to Yu Shun and the Xia. Is the Way of emperors and kings fundamentally recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals and in rites and music [?]? Thus the Six Classics are books, and what they contain is the Way. If these books are transmitted for one generation, the Way remains for one generation; if they are transmitted for ten generations, the Way remains for ten generations. If they are further transmitted for a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand generations, the Way likewise remains for those hundred, thousand, or ten thousand generations. Yet generations are still insufficient to measure its duration. The sun and moon shine perpetually, and this Way shines perpetually with them. The universe remains perpetually clear, and this Way remains perpetually clear with it. Mountains stand, rivers flow, and plants and trees flourish: does this Way not share the same constancy as their standing, flowing, and flourishing? Extend this reasoning to its utmost: Heaven and Earth are inexhaustible, and this Way is likewise inexhaustible with them.
Since the Way endures for ten thousand generations, its beneficent achievement endures for ten thousand generations. Scholars throughout those generations recite these books and transmit this Way, receiving the bounty of the sages and worthies even ten thousand generations later. Their hearts accord with the hearts of the sages and worthies, and their vital energies communicate with theirs. This is why scholars throughout the generations repay them with sacrifices without end, and why the institutions through which later kings honor virtue and recompense achievement grow ever more exalted and never fall into abeyance. From antiquity, the sages and worthies…

之在祀典者多矣。若黃帝、顓頊之法施於民，舜、鯀與冥之以身勤事，固有功於世者，然特施之當時耳。視孔子之刪詩書、定禮樂，以傳道於萬世者，其功為孰大？禹之以勞定國，湯、武之禦灾捍患，皆有功於世者，亦特用之當時耳。視孔子之贊周易、修春秋，以傳道於萬世者，其功為孰優？此宰我所以論夫子之事功曰：「賢於堯舜。」而周子亦曰：「夫子道德高厚，教化無窮，固宜萬世之王祀也。」論而至是，則知斯道之在天地間，必得聖賢而后明，非聖賢則不明也；必得聖賢而後行，非聖賢則不行也。道之所以明、所以行，皆本於聖賢。聖賢之功，其萬世之功也。斯道之傳於天地間，其所自之遠也如是夫！

抑又論之，周東遷而孔子生，推帝王之道以垂教後世，孔子固有功於帝王矣。宋南渡而朱子出，又註釋六經以覺我後人，朱子又有功於孔子矣。此所以
translation_en:
…who are included in the prescribed sacrifices are many. Huangdi and Zhuanxu extended their institutions to the people, while Shun, Gun, and Ming devoted themselves bodily to their duties. They certainly rendered service to the world, yet its benefits were confined to their own times. Compared with Kongzi, who edited the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents and established rites and music to transmit the Way to all generations, whose achievements were greater? Yu secured the realm through his labors, while Tang and Wu warded off calamities and defended against troubles. All rendered service to the world, yet its effects likewise belonged only to their own times. Compared with Kongzi, who elucidated the Changes of Zhou and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals to transmit the Way to all generations, whose achievements were superior? This is why Zai Wo, discussing the Master's deeds and achievements, said: “He surpassed Yao and Shun.” Master Zhou likewise said: “The Master's Way and virtue are lofty and profound, and his transforming instruction is inexhaustible. It is surely fitting that the kings of all generations offer sacrifices to him.” Having carried the argument this far, we know that this Way, existing between Heaven and Earth, requires sages and worthies to make it manifest; without them, it cannot be made manifest. It requires sages and worthies to put it into practice; without them, it cannot be practiced. Both the elucidation and the practice of the Way have their foundation in sages and worthies. Their achievements are achievements for all generations. Such is the distant origin of the transmission of this Way between Heaven and Earth!

Let us consider the matter further. After the Zhou moved east, Kongzi was born. He expounded the Way of the ancient emperors and kings, leaving instruction for later generations; thus Kongzi certainly rendered service to those emperors and kings. After the Song crossed south, Master Zhu emerged. He in turn annotated and explained the Six Classics to enlighten us of later generations; thus Master Zhu also rendered service to Kongzi. This is why…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
氣質蓋學莊而得其法度者此可與知者道也
考試官學士王批才氣沛然累千百言新意
層出讀之不厭蓋嘗用心韓蘇之學者歟
考試官學士徐批抑揚開闔法度森然讀之
累日不厭識者當自賞之得士如此亦可以為斯文喜矣
論曰以匹夫之身而垂無窮之澤其必有
所以為之者矣蓋人必有所以為之者然
後事可行而功可立苟無所以為之者則
吾所以自致者先無其本矣尚安望其能
===
有所成也哉何則得之者無自也體之者
無具也行之者無術也故夫世之人孰不
欲竊一善成一名以自立於天下然而無
所以為之者則雖僅得於一時而不能垂
於身後能垂於身後而不能延及於萬世
之遠此不得其所以為之者故也蓋物之
存乎天者理有固然而事之出乎人者每
有不可必得嗚呼古之聖賢以匹夫而垂
無窮之澤其本源之地施為之體運用之

氣質，蓋學莊而得其法度者，此可與知者道也。

論曰：以匹夫之身而垂無窮之澤，其必有所以為之者矣。蓋人必有所以為之者，然後事可行而功可立。苟無所以為之者，則吾所以自致者先無其本矣，尚安望其能有所成也哉？何則？得之者無自也，體之者無具也，行之者無術也。故夫世之人，孰不欲竊一善、成一名，以自立於天下？然而無所以為之者，則雖僅得於一時，而不能垂於身後；能垂於身後，而不能延及於萬世之遠。此不得其所以為之者故也。蓋物之存乎天者，理有固然；而事之出乎人者，每有不可必得。嗚呼！古之聖賢以匹夫而垂無窮之澤，其本源之地、施為之體、運用之
translation_en:
…the manner characteristic of examination writing. Evidently he has studied Zhuangzi and mastered his methods and standards. This is something one can discuss with those who understand.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician: His talent and spirit flow abundantly. Through thousands upon hundreds of words, fresh ideas emerge one after another, and one never tires of reading. Has he perhaps devoted himself to studying Han Yu and Su Shi?

Comment by Examiner Xu, Academician: In its rising and falling, opening and closing, the composition displays rigorous command of method. One can read it for days without tiring. Discerning readers will surely appreciate it for themselves. To obtain a scholar such as this is indeed cause for rejoicing in our literary tradition.

The discourse reads: For a man of common status to leave benefits that endure without end, he must surely possess the means to accomplish this. Only when a person possesses such means can undertakings be carried out and achievements established. If he lacks them, then his own efforts to attain distinction lack their foundation from the outset. How could one still expect him to accomplish anything? Why is this? His attainment has no source; his embodiment of it has no means; his practice of it has no method. Who in this world does not wish to lay claim to some good deed and establish a reputation, thereby securing a standing in the world? Yet without the means to accomplish this, even if he gains something for a time, he cannot transmit it beyond his death; even if he can transmit it beyond his death, he cannot extend it to the distant reach of ten thousand generations. This is because he has not grasped the means by which it is accomplished. For things that subsist in Heaven, principle has its inherent certainty; but in affairs that proceed from human beings, the desired result often cannot be assured. Alas! The sages and worthies of antiquity, though men of common status, left benefits that endure without end. As for the ground of their ultimate source, the substance of their activity, and the ways in which they put it into operation…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
方盖必有原乎天具乎心通造化之變妙
萬物之故不待生而存不隨往而亡者矣
天下尊之萬世尊之其澤與天地並而其
受天下之報也亦與天地並斯理之固然
者聖賢道在萬世朱子之論盖有見於聖
賢之所以為聖賢者請申其說人之一身
甚微也生於一時甚近也天下甚大也以
天下之大而至於萬世甚遠也二者若邈
乎其不相關也聖賢者亦人耳而何其道
===
之在於萬世也嗚呼聖賢之為聖賢其必
有所以為之者矣一氣之相為流通自太
極而來至于今不易也日月之在天至於
今明也江河之在地至于今流也山嶽至
于今峙草木禽獸虫魚至于今蕃且育也
是氣使之然也而道實為之道也者運行
於氣之中而主乎是氣者也天不變道亦
不變是道出乎天又必有所为主之者以
經綸其大經立其大本而妙其化育以裁

經合其大經立其大本而妙其化育以裁
punctuated:
方，盖必有原乎天、具乎心、通造化之變、妙萬物之故，不待生而存、不隨往而亡者矣。天下尊之，萬世尊之，其澤與天地並，而其受天下之報也，亦與天地並，斯理之固然者。「聖賢道在萬世」，朱子之論，盖有見於聖賢之所以為聖賢者。請申其說：人之一身甚微也，生於一時甚近也；天下甚大也，以天下之大而至於萬世甚遠也。二者若邈乎其不相關也。聖賢者亦人耳，而何其道之在於萬世也？

嗚呼！聖賢之為聖賢，其必有所以為之者矣。一氣之相為流通，自太極而來，至于今不易也。日月之在天，至於今明也；江河之在地，至于今流也；山嶽至于今峙，草木禽獸虫魚至于今蕃且育也。是氣使之然也，而道實為之。道也者，運行於氣之中而主乎是氣者也。天不變，道亦不變。是道出乎天，又必有所为主之者，以經綸其大經，立其大本，而妙其化育，以裁
translation_en:
…methods must surely possess something that originates in Heaven, is fully present in the heart-mind, comprehends the transformations of creation, and subtly grasps the workings of the myriad things—something that exists without awaiting their birth and does not perish with their passing. All under Heaven revere them, and ten thousand generations revere them. Their beneficence ranks alongside Heaven and Earth, and the recompense they receive from all under Heaven likewise ranks alongside Heaven and Earth. This is necessarily so according to principle. In saying, “The Way of the sages and worthies endures for ten thousand generations,” Master Zhu evidently perceived what makes sages and worthies what they are. Allow me to elaborate upon his account. A single human being is exceedingly small, and a life confined to one age is exceedingly brief. All under Heaven is exceedingly vast, and its extension through ten thousand generations is exceedingly remote. The two seem so far apart as to have no connection. Sages and worthies are also merely human: how, then, does their Way endure for ten thousand generations?

Ah! There must surely be something that makes sages and worthies what they are. The single vital force, qi, circulates throughout all things; from the Supreme Ultimate down to the present, it has remained unchanged. The sun and moon in the heavens shine to this day; the rivers upon the earth flow to this day; the mountains stand to this day; and plants, birds, beasts, insects, and fish flourish and reproduce to this day. This vital force makes them so, yet it is the Way that truly brings this about. The Way operates within vital force and governs it. Heaven does not change, and neither does the Way. This Way issues from Heaven, and there must also be someone who presides over it, ordering its great guiding principles, establishing its great foundation, and bringing its transforming and nourishing powers to their subtle fulfillment, so as to fashion…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
成輔相於天下以參乎天地於無窮者歟
者非聖賢而何天以是付之聖賢聖賢以
是而受之於天夫豈苟然者使其苟然也
則天之生聖賢必不如是其不多見也聖
賢之生亦必不如是其甚異於斯人也其
所得必不如是其大而所自任必不如是
其重也其所及必不如是其遠也是故其
必有所以為之者矣夫人皆有言也言則
為法夫人皆有行也行則為度夫人皆有
===
動也動則為道耳目一也其視則明其聽
則聰心志一也其思則睿其謀則哲人倫
一也其君臣則義其父子則親其長幼則
序其夫婦則別其朋友則信其知先知其
覺先覺也其義理則先得我心之所同然
也猶規矩焉而方與圓之至也猶準繩焉
而平與直之至也所謂出類拔萃者在是
所謂首出庶物而卓冠羣倫者在是夫聖
賢者何以得此哉蓋必有所以為之者也
alt_text:
成輔於天下以奉乎天地於無窮者與
者非聖賢而何天以是付之聖賢聖賢以
是而受之於天夫豈苟然者使其苟然也
則天之生聖賢必不如是其不多見也聖
賢之生亦必不如是其甚異於斯人也其
所得必不如是甚大而所自任必不如是
其重也其所及必不如是其遠也是故其
必有所以為之者矣夫人皆有言也言則
為法夫人皆有行也行則為度夫人皆有
===
動也動則為道耳目一也其視則明其聽
則聰心志一也其思則睿其謀則哲人倫
一也其君臣則義其父子則親其長幼則
序其夫婦則別其朋友則信其知先知其
覺先覺也其義理則先得我心之所同然
也猶規矩焉而方與圓之至也猶準繩焉
而平與直之至也所謂出類拔萃者在是
所謂首出庶物而卓冠羣倫者在是夫聖
賢者何以得此哉蓋必有所以為之者也
punctuated:
成輔相於天下，以參乎天地於無窮者歟？者非聖賢而何？天以是付之聖賢，聖賢以是而受之於天，夫豈苟然者？使其苟然也，則天之生聖賢，必不如是其不多見也；聖賢之生，亦必不如是其甚異於斯人也。其所得必不如是其大，而所自任必不如是其重也，其所及必不如是其遠也。是故其必有所以為之者矣。
夫人皆有言也，言則為法；夫人皆有行也，行則為度；夫人皆有動也，動則為道。耳目一也，其視則明，其聽則聰；心志一也，其思則睿，其謀則哲；人倫一也，其君臣則義，其父子則親，其長幼則序，其夫婦則別，其朋友則信。其知先知，其覺先覺也；其義理則先得我心之所同然也。猶規矩焉，而方與圓之至也；猶準繩焉，而平與直之至也。所謂出類拔萃者在是，所謂首出庶物而卓冠羣倫者在是。夫聖賢者何以得此哉？蓋必有所以為之者也。
translation_en:
…bring to completion and assist these processes throughout the world, thereby participating with Heaven and Earth without end? Who could do this but sages and worthies? [?] Heaven entrusts this to sages and worthies, and sages and worthies receive it from Heaven. How could this be a matter of chance? If it were chance, then Heaven’s bringing forth sages and worthies would surely not be so rare, nor would the sages and worthies who are born differ so greatly from other people. What they have received would surely not be so great; the responsibilities they take upon themselves would not be so weighty; and their influence would not reach so far. Thus there must be something that makes them what they are.
All people speak, yet the words of sages and worthies become models; all people act, yet their conduct becomes a standard; all people move, yet their movements embody the Way. Their ears and eyes are the same as other people’s, yet their sight is clear and their hearing keen. Their minds and intentions are the same, yet their thought is penetrating and their deliberation wise. Their human relationships are the same, yet between ruler and minister they uphold righteousness; between father and son, affection; between elder and younger, due order; between husband and wife, distinction; and between friends, trustworthiness. In knowledge, they know before others; in understanding, they awaken before others. In moral principles, they grasp before us what our hearts alike acknowledge as right. They are like the compass and square, the ultimate standards of roundness and squareness; like the level and marking line, the ultimate standards of evenness and straightness. Herein lies what is meant by rising above one’s kind and standing out from the multitude; herein lies what is meant by emerging foremost among all beings and towering above one’s fellows. How do sages and worthies attain this? Surely there must be something that makes them what they are.

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
非人也天也是故大而化之之謂聖大而
將至於化之之謂賢雖其微有不同而其
所得乎天者一也聖賢以其受於天者為
天地立心為生民立命為往聖繼絕學為
萬世開太平以一身為天下計天下猶一
身也以一時為萬世計萬世猶一時也仁
之親行於萬世之父子義之敬行於萬世
之君臣禮之序智之別信之交際行於萬
世之長幼夫婦朋友詩書之文載此道以
===

法度防閑乎此道也典禮命討鼓舞乎此
道也異端之塞路也而闢之吾道廓如矣
邪說之移人也而放之吾道卓如矣是故
天地之間自古至今日月之所以長明江
河之所以長流山嶽之所以長峙草木禽

translation_en: …It is not human in origin; it comes from Heaven. Thus, one who is great and has become transformed is called a sage; one who is great and is approaching transformation is called a worthy. Although they differ slightly, what they receive from Heaven is the same. Through what they receive from Heaven, sages and worthies establish a heart for Heaven and Earth, establish a destiny for the living people, continue the interrupted learning of past sages, and inaugurate peace for all generations. In their own persons they plan for all under Heaven, treating all under Heaven as a single body; in their own age they plan for all generations, treating all generations as a single age. The affection of benevolence operates between fathers and sons through all generations; the respect of righteousness operates between rulers and ministers through all generations; and the ordering of ritual propriety, the distinctions of wisdom, and the intercourse of trustworthiness operate respectively between older and younger, husbands and wives, and friends through all generations. The writings of the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents carry this Way and transmit it; the institutions of ritual and music give this Way regulated expression and put it into practice. Punishments, government, laws, and standards safeguard this Way; canonical rites, appointments, and punitive measures encourage people to follow it. When heterodox teachings block the road, sages and worthies refute them, and our Way becomes open and expansive; when pernicious doctrines sway people, they banish them, and our Way stands supreme. Thus, between Heaven and Earth, from antiquity to the present, the sun and moon have continued to shine, rivers have continued to flow, mountains have continued to tower, and plants, birds, beasts, insects, and fish have continued to multiply and grow: who has made this so? Dwellings in palaces and houses, clothing of hemp, food of rice, millet, vegetables, fruit, fish, and meat, sustenance for the living, burial for the dead, distinctions between superior and inferior, gradations between noble and lowly, farmers and artisans…

然則聖賢也有莫大之功於斯民其享萬

translation_en:
…and the profit-making activities of merchants: who brought these about? It was the Way of the six sages. Thus the sages rendered the greatest service to the people. Is it not fitting that they should receive sacrifices for ten thousand generations, and that the people should forever give the fullest expression to their wish to commemorate distant ancestors and repay their benefactors? I maintain that this rests with Heaven and does not originate with human beings. Alas! After the rulers known as the Two Emperors and Three Kings, the scholars Confucius and Mencius arose. Had Heaven not brought forth these men, we would long since have worn our robes fastened on the left, like the barbarians. Nevertheless, the Two Emperors and Three Kings put the Way into practice in their own time, while Confucius and Mencius transmitted it to later ages. Without Confucius and Mencius, the Way of those emperors and kings would not have been made clear. Thus the achievements of Confucius and Mencius far surpassed those of Yao and Shun, and greatly exceeded those of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. In the Song dynasty, the scholars of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min arose in succession, and the Way of Confucius and Mencius once again shone brightly throughout the world. Did these scholars not also assist Confucius and Mencius, rendering service that would endure for ten thousand generations? Master Shao, known as Kangjie, said: “Zhongni took ten thousand generations as his domain.” I would say the same of these scholars.

We humbly consider that the transmission of the teaching of holding fast to the mean is recorded in the Classics, revealing the subtleties of the emperors’ and kings’ methods of cultivating the mind; the achievements of good government survive in the histories, illuminating the deeds and accomplishments of worthy and wise men. Thus, when expounding the Way at the Classics Colloquium, one should give thoughtful attention to historical writings. Moreover, among rulers of more recent times who devoted themselves energetically to government, Taizong of the Tang alone was preeminent. The Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Reign (Zhenguan zhengyao) was indeed compiled by the court historian Wu Jing. Arranged by subject into ten juan, it preserves historical precedents in full. His renown stands foremost among the three revered emperors [?], and later generations look up to him with admiration.
His achievements in repelling the foreign peoples and bringing peace to the Chinese realm shine like the sun and stars; his sincerity in employing worthy men and accepting remonstrance is manifest as a tortoise-shell oracle or a mirror. The admonitions exchanged between ruler and ministers never departed from benevolence, righteousness, the Way, and virtue; the deliberations of superiors and subordinates likewise approached the ideal of upright and enlightened undertakings. Beginning with “The Way of the Ruler” and “The Structure of Government,” the work sets out its main principles and unfolds their particulars; concluding with “Calamities and Auspicious Signs” and “Taking Care to the End,” it distinguishes and analyzes each matter in detail. Whether its language is ornate or plain, its import lies in encouragement and admonition. Matters of military and civil government are comprehensively presented, and the ordering of human affairs is fully treated. Truly, it is an exemplary work from a former dynasty…

…and may be put into practice in this sage age. We reverently consider that Your Majesty, 〇〇〇〇 [?], sagely and divine, accomplished in civil and martial affairs, impartial and upright, reverent and dignified, presides over an age of flourishing achievement and continues the legacy of the one founding ancestor and four imperial forebears. Your mind abides in profound stillness, following the standards of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors. You care for the people as though they were wounded and seek the Way as though you had yet to glimpse it. You continually illuminate your sagely learning, nourishing your mind with ancient teachings; you grandly extend the imperial enterprise, drawing upon this book to aid your government.
Amid the respite from your myriad affairs, you once commanded that this book be expounded and examined, requiring that even an error in a single character be corrected. Directions issued from your imperial judgment, and writing materials were supplied by the imperial workshops. Among the prefatory writings, that of Wu Cheng received foremost attention; the textual investigations and explanations of Ge Zhi were also included. Your brilliant imperial composition, splendid as heavenly blossoms, stands as a preface at the beginning of the volume. Brocade covers and precious cases prepare it for the gaze of your imperial double pupils, the mark of a sage ruler. We, 〔your servant, So-and-so〕 and the others, undeservedly hold posts in your attendance and discharge duties of deliberation and reflection. In literary talent we fall short of the master of Meishan, and have yet to submit a memorial on the Tang minister [?]; in learning we fall short of Zuyu, yet venture to present a composition on imperial learning. We humbly pray that you select its essential sayings and display them…

Take goodness as your teacher and other people as your mirror, finding here some assistance in journeying far and ascending high, and some infinitesimal aid in extending your sight and hearing. We further hope that you will immerse yourself in Heaven’s workings, which have neither sound nor scent, and remain reverent and cautious even where nothing is seen or heard; take the sages of antiquity as your teachers, apprehend ultimate principle in the Six Classics, faithfully follow the great Way, and surpass the flourishing rule of the Three Dynasties. We, your servants So-and-so and the others, look toward Heaven and gaze up in reverence at Your Sageliness with the utmost fervor and trembling awe. We respectfully submit, together with this memorial, the text we have collated of Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Reign of the Tang (Tang Zhenguan zhengyao), for Your Majesty’s attention.

Associate Examiner Wang, Junior Compiler, comments: “The general principles and definitions of the penal code are difficult even for seasoned officials, yet this candidate handles them with the greatest ease in this policy essay. Would he consent to bear out Master Su’s words about having no means to guide his ruler? Discerning readers regret that his other compositions have not all been included. Yet these are like pearls bright enough to illuminate a carriage: to obtain even one is enough.”

Associate Examiner Shang, Junior Compiler, comments: “His answers to the five policy questions are detailed and ample, like jade heaped in Xuanpu, shining brilliantly in the night. If put into practice, all would prove eminently workable. It is regrettable that we cannot present them all, but we still look forward to his fuller and more splendid exposition in his response at the imperial court.”

Associate Examiner Wu, Senior Compiler, comments: “His talent and understanding are outstanding; reading his work is invigorating. We have selected only the first essay to give a sense of the others. Those with a discerning eye should recognize that its excellence lies in more than simply remembering historical facts. That this examination has discovered a worthy scholar is the common judgment. The phoenix soars a thousand fathoms high: how gratifying to behold it contemplating the radiance of virtue at the court of Yu and becoming an auspicious sign of an age of good government!”

Examiner Wang, Academician, comments: “He answers each question as it comes, flowing freely without impediment, while his literary brilliance shines forth. He must be a man of extensive learning.”

Examiner Xu, Academician, comments: “He knows both antiquity and the present, and possesses both learning and discernment. These shine brilliantly through his writing and pour forth as though inexhaustible. Can scholars such as this be found in any great number?”

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
乎民而為制治之用此我
朝
列聖垂世立教之典明刑弼教之章愚生所以
日夜莊誦而不敢偏廢者也夫
三誥三書家傳人誦
奎章宸翰昭回于天與六經相表裏
神謀聖訓流行於世與三代為後先固無俟
於言矣惟大明律一書則古人沿革之異

translation_en:
…the people and serve as the practical means of establishing good government. These are the canons through which the successive sage emperors of our dynasty have handed down instruction to posterity, and the writings through which they have clarified punishments to support moral teaching. This is why I, an unworthy student, reverently recite them day and night, not daring to neglect either aspect. The Three Proclamations and the Three Books are transmitted in every household and recited by everyone. These imperial compositions and writings shine across the heavens, complementing the Six Classics; their divine counsels and sagely instructions circulate throughout the world, continuing the achievements of the Three Dynasties. These things surely require no further discussion.
As for the single work, the Great Ming Code, however, the differences in what earlier generations retained or changed, and the thoroughness with which these matters have now been examined and settled, truly demand study. The earlier Confucian master Cheng said that the Five Classics contain the Spring and Autumn Annals just as statutory law contains precedents for adjudication. Why is this so? The Five Classics set forth enduring precepts, much as statutory law does; the Spring and Autumn Annals conveys judgments of censure, much as judicial precedents do. In refinement and coarseness, scope and scale, they are certainly far apart. Yet the Five Classics are in fact the original source of statutory law, and the Spring and Autumn Annals is the essential model for judicial precedents. In this respect, they have never been dissimilar.
As for framing punishments according to the natural human relationships, this expressed the generous and sincere intentions of Yu and Zhou; invoking the Classics to decide judicial cases, however, was a theory based on strained connections made by Han Confucians. When Shang Yang changed the designation fa to lü, books of statutes first acquired that name; when Ling Lun cut bamboo into pitch pipes, called lü, the meaning of the term was first established. Zichan cast the penal code in metal, and Li Kui compiled the Canon of Laws. The Han had its Nine Chapters, and the Wei its Eighteen Chapters; the Qi and Liang…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
而下不暇數也唐有䟽議宋有格式胡元
之世不足論也笞杖徒流死今之五刑也
而墨劓剕宮大辟非虞周之五刑乎議親
議故議功議賢議能議勤議貴議賓今之
八議也而不孝不睦不婣不弟不任不恤
造言亂民非周之八刑乎今之三流列於
五刑之中虞之五流宥於五刑之外以准
皆各其及即若之八字今律例分則因於
隋名例衛禁職制戶婚等十一類今律損
===
益則本於唐此古今之律可見者槩如此
雖然唐律尚有可議者其比類未周分合
無統如妻無七出義絕離之之分為二袒
免以上之親有本宗外姻之異而混為一
盜賊槩収乎人命職制並取乎贓賕若此
者不一而足今律皆釐而正之嗚呼制雖
出於前代而良法悉斷乎
聖心之淵微事雖循乎百王而美意必存乎
宸衷之欽恤此今律之所以獨超於唐而並

punctuated:
而下，不暇數也。唐有䟽議，宋有格式，胡元之世不足論也。笞、杖、徒、流、死，今之五刑也，而墨、劓、剕、宮、大辟，非虞周之五刑乎？議親、議故、議功、議賢、議能、議勤、議貴、議賓，今之八議也，而不孝、不睦、不婣、不弟、不任、不恤、造言、亂民，非周之八刑乎？今之三流列於五刑之中，虞之五流宥於五刑之外。以准、皆、各、其、及、即、若、之八字，今律例分則因於隋；名例、衛禁、職制、戶婚等十一類，今律損益則本於唐。此古今之律可見者，槩如此。
雖然，唐律尚有可議者：其比類未周，分合無統。如妻無七出義絕離之之分為二，袒免以上之親有本宗外姻之異而混為一；盜賊槩収乎人命，職制並取乎贓賕，若此者不一而足。今律皆釐而正之。嗚呼！制雖出於前代，而良法悉斷乎聖心之淵微；事雖循乎百王，而美意必存乎宸衷之欽恤。此今律之所以獨超於唐而並
translation_en:
…and thereafter, there is no time to enumerate them all. The Tang had the Code with Commentary; the Song had regulations and ordinances. The age of the non-Chinese Yuan does not merit discussion. Beating with the light stick, beating with the heavy stick, penal servitude, exile, and death are the present Five Punishments. Were tattooing, cutting off the nose, amputation of the feet, castration, and capital punishment not the Five Punishments of Yu and Zhou? Deliberation for relatives of the sovereign, old associates, the meritorious, the worthy, the able, the diligent, the noble, and honored guests constitutes the present Eight Deliberations. Were unfilial conduct, discord among kin, discord among relatives by marriage, failure in fraternal duty, failure of trustworthiness, lack of compassion, fabrication of rumors, and disordering the people not the eight offenses punished by the Zhou? The present three degrees of exile fall within the Five Punishments; the five forms of exile under Yu provided mitigation outside the Five Punishments. In the distinctions made in its rules through the eight characters 准, 皆, 各, 其, 及, 即, 若, and 之, the present code follows the Sui. In its eleven categories, including General Principles, Palace Guards and Prohibitions, Administrative Regulations, and Households and Marriage, the present code takes the Tang as its basis, with additions and omissions. Such, in broad outline, is what can be discerned concerning ancient and present codes.
Nevertheless, the Tang Code still has points open to criticism: its classification by analogy is incomplete, and its divisions and combinations lack a consistent organizing principle. For example, it separates into two provisions divorcing a wife who has committed none of the seven grounds for repudiation and divorcing her where marital obligations have been severed [?]. It conflates into one category relatives for whom mourning is prescribed at the degree of baring the arm and wearing the mourning headband or above, despite the distinction between paternal kin and maternal or affinal kin. Theft and robbery are indiscriminately grouped with homicide, and administrative regulations are grouped with illicit gains and bribes. Such instances are too numerous to list. The present code has disentangled and corrected them all. Ah! Although its institutions derive from earlier dynasties, its sound laws are all determined by the profound discernment of the imperial mind. Although its practices follow those of the hundred kings, its beneficent intent necessarily resides in the sovereign’s reverent care and compassion. This is why the present code uniquely surpasses that of the Tang and stands alongside…

駕於虞周之隆也。
三誥三書所以為教，《大明律》一書所以為政。制治保邦，勸善懲惡，成四海之治，垂萬世之統，列聖之制作規模宏遠矣。《書》曰：「有典有則，貽厥子孫。」敢敬為祖宗頌。《詩》曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」則請為今日聖天子獻也。夫讀書而不知律，謂之迂儒；讀律而不知書，謂之俗吏。愚也固不敢不通時務而流於儒之迂，亦不忍專事簿書而陷於吏之俗。執事倘幸進焉，使得效用明時，以行幼學之志，則三誥三書之道、一律之法，愚雖不敏，不敢不慎。

translation_en:
…to stand alongside the flourishing ages of Yu and Zhou.
The Three Announcements and the Three Writings serve to instruct; the single work, the Great Ming Code, serves to govern. Establishing order and safeguarding the realm, encouraging good and punishing evil, bringing orderly government to all within the Four Seas and transmitting a ruling tradition for ten thousand generations—the institutions created by the successive sage emperors are grand in scope and far-reaching in design. The Book of Documents says: “There are statutes and rules, bequeathed to their descendants.” I respectfully venture to offer this in praise of the imperial ancestors. The Book of Odes says: “Neither transgressing nor forgetting, following the old statutes.” This I beg to offer to the sage Son of Heaven of the present day. Those who read the classics but do not understand the laws are called impractical scholars; those who read the laws but do not understand the classics are called vulgar clerks. Foolish though I am, I certainly dare not remain ignorant of contemporary affairs and lapse into scholarly impracticality; nor can I bear to devote myself exclusively to registers and documents and sink into clerical vulgarity. Should you, honored examiners, graciously advance me, enabling me to render service in this enlightened age and fulfill the aspirations formed in my youthful studies, then, though I lack ability, I would not dare to be careless in applying the principles of the Three Announcements and the Three Writings and the provisions of the Code.

Chen Xuan

They merely picked up historical precedents by listening surreptitiously to others and used these to elaborate upon the question’s wording; their discussions were so vague that one could neither affirm nor reject them [?]…

正如矮人觀塲隨衆悲喜殊可笑也絕響之餘乃有此卷
慧可謂希聲也夫

見該博且筆勢如風檣陣馬其氣充矣

對聖人有和平天下之具而必有和平天
===
下之本蓋天下和平治之極也禮樂刑政
何者非治天下之具然而生民之道樂為
大焉則所以和平天下者在此而不在彼
矣執事發策下詢以四者並言而獨致詳
於樂良以是歟愚竊以為心和則氣和氣
和則形和形和然後天地之和應而樂可
作也然則聖人之和平天下不徒恃其具
而必本諸心也彰彰矣請因明問所及而
條陳之昔者聖人之治天下禮以道其志

考試官學士徐批：問目頗多，此子歷歷能道，其亦博聞強記者歟？
對：聖人有和平天下之具，而必有和平天下之本。蓋天下和平，治之極也。禮樂刑政，何者非治天下之具？然而生民之道，樂為大焉，則所以和平天下者在此而不在彼矣。執事發策下詢，以四者並言，而獨致詳於樂，良以是歟？愚竊以為心和則氣和，氣和則形和，形和然後天地之和應，而樂可作也。然則聖人之和平天下，不徒恃其具，而必本諸心也，彰彰矣。請因明問所及而條陳之。昔者聖人之治天下，禮以道其志，
translation_en:
…just like a short man watching a performance, sharing the crowd’s sorrow and joy: truly laughable. After worthy voices had fallen silent, this script has appeared; it may indeed be called a rare sound! [The character 慧 here is doubtful.]

Associate Examiner Liu, a Compiler, comments: All five policy essays answer their questions well, but this piece especially displays comprehensive learning. Moreover, its writing moves like wind-driven masts and horses charging in formation: its vital force is abundant.

Examiner Wang, an Academician, comments: Precise and thorough in examining precedents, orderly and fluent in composition—a fine work.

Examiner Xu, an Academician, comments: The question contains quite a number of topics, yet this candidate can discuss each distinctly. Surely he is a man of wide learning and retentive memory!

In reply: The sage possesses the instruments for bringing peace and harmony to all under Heaven, but he must also possess the foundation for doing so. Peace and harmony throughout the world are the highest achievement of government. Ritual, music, punishments, and administration—which of these is not an instrument for governing the world? Yet in the Way of nurturing the people, music is paramount. Thus the means of bringing peace and harmony to the world lie in this rather than in the others. In setting this policy question and graciously soliciting answers, you mention all four together, yet address music alone in particular detail. Is this indeed the reason?

I humbly believe that when the heart is harmonious, the vital energy is harmonious; when the vital energy is harmonious, the bodily form is harmonious. Only when the bodily form is harmonious does the harmony of Heaven and Earth respond, and music can then be made. It is therefore abundantly clear that, in bringing peace and harmony to the world, the sage does not merely rely upon these instruments, but must take the heart as his foundation. Allow me to address in sequence the matters covered by your illuminating question. In antiquity, when the sages governed the world, they used ritual to guide the people’s intentions…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
樂以和其聲政以一其行刑以防其姦禮
樂刑政四達而不悖則天下治矣然而安
上治民莫善於禮移風易俗莫善於樂故
聖人雖不能不道之以政齊之以刑而禮
樂二者尤加之意焉自夫嬴秦取之以詐
力守之以詐力則所謂刑政者皆非先王
之舊況於禮樂乎然禮猶有存者而樂則
無聞焉雅樂文舞僅見於郊廟而未嘗用
之邦國僅見於朝廷而未嘗達之天下偏
===
州下邑終老而不知其器無怪也雖然胡
部俗樂導欲增悲則又不若無之之為愈
矣洪惟
國朝
太祖高皇帝即位之初他務未遑既命牛諒制
禮復命陶凱典樂以一心之和而致天下
之和以天下之和被之音聲之和自是以
來
聖聖相承而守一道禮樂可謂明備矣然而猶

punctuated:
樂以和其聲，政以一其行，刑以防其姦。禮樂刑政，四達而不悖，則天下治矣。然而安上治民，莫善於禮；移風易俗，莫善於樂。故聖人雖不能不道之以政、齊之以刑，而禮樂二者尤加之意焉。自夫嬴秦取之以詐力，守之以詐力，則所謂刑政者皆非先王之舊，況於禮樂乎？然禮猶有存者，而樂則無聞焉。雅樂文舞僅見於郊廟，而未嘗用之邦國；僅見於朝廷，而未嘗達之天下。偏州下邑，終老而不知其器，無怪也。雖然，胡部俗樂，導欲增悲，則又不若無之之為愈矣。
洪惟國朝太祖高皇帝即位之初，他務未遑，既命牛諒制禮，復命陶凱典樂。以一心之和而致天下之和，以天下之和被之音聲之和。自是以來，聖聖相承而守一道，禮樂可謂明備矣。然而猶
translation_en:
…music to harmonize their voices, government to unify their conduct, and punishments to prevent their wrongdoing. When rites, music, punishments, and government all operate throughout the realm without conflicting, the world is well governed. Yet nothing surpasses rites for securing those above and governing the people, and nothing surpasses music for transforming prevailing ways and changing customs. Thus, although the sages could not dispense with guiding the people through government and regulating them through punishments, they devoted particular attention to rites and music. Once the Ying house of Qin seized the realm through deceit and force and maintained it through deceit and force, what were called punishments and government no longer followed the ancient practices of the former kings. How much less could rites and music have done so? Yet some rites still survived, whereas music went unheard. Elegant music and civil dances appeared only at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, never being employed throughout the states; they appeared only at court, never reaching the whole realm. It is no wonder that people in remote prefectures and humble towns could grow old without knowing these instruments. Nevertheless, the popular music of the foreign ensembles arouses desire and deepens sorrow: it would be better to have no such music at all.
We reverently reflect that, at the beginning of the reign of our dynasty’s Emperor Taizu Gao, before he had leisure for other affairs, he commanded Niu Liang to establish rites and then commanded Tao Kai to take charge of music. Through the harmony of his own heart, he brought about harmony throughout the realm; he then expressed the realm’s harmony in harmonious musical sounds. Since then, sage sovereign has succeeded sage sovereign, upholding a single Way, and rites and music may be said to be clearly established and fully provided. Nevertheless, there still…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
有未盡復古者非不欲復古也黄帝堯舜
通變宜民亦必歷數聖人然後備耳昔魯
兩生有言禮樂積德百年而後興自
國初至今百有餘年矣况乎
今上以聖人之德在
天子之位則斟酌損益成
列聖之緒而使之盡善盡美者天下不能無望
焉雖然傅說不云乎事不師古匪說攸聞
則歷代之樂載諸典籍者不可不考矣盖
===
黄帝之樂曰雲門大卷以其能成名萬物
以明民其德如雲之出也帝堯之樂曰大
咸咸池以其能善均刑法以儀民其德無
所不施也舜之德能紹放勳故謂之大韶
禹之德能大中國故謂之大夏大濩者湯
之樂非以其德能救斯民乎大武者武之
樂非以其德能成武功乎至若伏羲之樂
名立基神農之樂名下謀祝融之樂曰属
續少皞之樂曰九淵雖世尚洪荒命名之

黄帝之樂曰雲門大卷以其能成名萬物
以明民其德如雲之出也帝堯之樂曰大
咸咸池以其能善均刑法以儀民其德無
所不施也舜之德能紹敘勳故謂之大韶
禹之德能大中國故謂之大夏大濩者湯
之樂非以其德能救斯民乎大武者武之
樂非以其德能成武功乎至若伏羲之樂
名立本神農之樂名下謀祝融之樂曰屬
續少皞之樂曰九淵顓頊尚帝命名之
punctuated:
有未盡復古者，非不欲復古也。黄帝、堯、舜通變宜民，亦必歷數聖人然後備耳。昔魯兩生有言：「禮樂積德百年而後興。」自國初至今百有餘年矣。况乎今上以聖人之德在天子之位，則斟酌損益，成列聖之緒，而使之盡善盡美者，天下不能無望焉。雖然，傅說不云乎：「事不師古，匪說攸聞。」則歷代之樂載諸典籍者，不可不考矣。
盖黄帝之樂曰雲門、大卷，以其能成名萬物以明民，其德如雲之出也。帝堯之樂曰大咸、咸池，以其能善均刑法以儀民，其德無所不施也。舜之德能紹放勳，故謂之大韶；禹之德能大中國，故謂之大夏。大濩者，湯之樂，非以其德能救斯民乎？大武者，武之樂，非以其德能成武功乎？至若伏羲之樂名立基，神農之樂名下謀，祝融之樂曰属續，少皞之樂曰九淵，雖世尚洪荒，命名之
translation_en:
…there are still respects in which ancient practice has not been fully restored; this is not because there is no desire to restore it. Even the adaptations made by Huangdi, Yao, and Shun to suit the people had to pass through several sages before reaching completion. Once, the two scholars of Lu said: “Rites and music arise only after virtue has accumulated for a hundred years.” More than a hundred years have now passed since the founding of our dynasty. Moreover, His present Majesty occupies the position of Son of Heaven with the virtue of a sage. The realm cannot but hope that he will weigh what should be diminished or augmented, complete the work of the successive sage emperors, and bring it to utter goodness and perfection. Yet did not Fu Yue say, “Undertaking affairs without taking antiquity as a model is something of which I, Yue, have never heard”? Thus the music of successive ages, as recorded in the classical writings, must be examined.
Huangdi’s music was called Cloud Gate (Yunmen) and Great Scroll (Dajuan), because he could bring the myriad things to completion and give them names, thereby enlightening the people; his virtue was like clouds emerging. Emperor Yao’s music was called Great Universality (Daxian) and Universal Pool (Xianchi), because he could make punishments and laws equitable and thereby provide a standard for the people; there was nowhere his virtue did not extend. Shun’s virtue could continue the work of Fangxun [Yao], so his music was called Great Continuation (Dashao). Yu’s virtue could enlarge the Central States, so his music was called Great Xia (Daxia). Great Protection (Dahuo) was Tang’s music: was this not because his virtue could save these people? Great Martial Achievement (Dawu) was King Wu’s music: was this not because his virtue could accomplish martial deeds? As for Fuxi’s music, it was named Establishing the Foundation (Liji); Shennong’s music was named Lower Counsel (Xiamou) [?]; Zhurong’s music was called Continuation (Shuxu); and Shaohao’s music was called Nine Depths (Jiuyuan). Although their ages still belonged to remote antiquity, the meaning of these names…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
義不傳然先聖後聖崇德之義則一蓋可
想見也夫數聖人之樂皆所以崇德則其
和平天下不徒有其具而實有其本矣由
漢而唐由唐而宋雖制禮作樂代不乏人
然其去聖人也不亦遠乎以漢言之高帝
之時叔孫通因秦樂人作宗廟樂唐山夫
人因帝好楚聲作房中樂至武帝東封泰
山還坐明堂其臣兒寬又請作神樂焉以
唐言之高祖定天下命祖孝孫等作雅樂
===
太宗平東都破宋金剛等作凱樂至高宗
時景雲見河水清其臣張文收又作燕樂
焉迨至有宋乾德樂作於太祖太常和峴
之所定也萬國朝天樂平晉樂作於太宗
郊廟祭享之所用也至仁宗因王堯臣之
請則又有大安樂大晟樂焉凡若此者或
襲先代之弊陋或宣一時之侈心先後一
律也夫數君之樂非出於崇德則其和平
天下不徒無其本亦且無其具矣若乃諧

punctuated: 義不傳，然先聖後聖崇德之義則一，蓋可想見也。夫數聖人之樂皆所以崇德，則其和平天下，不徒有其具，而實有其本矣。由漢而唐，由唐而宋，雖制禮作樂，代不乏人，然其去聖人也，不亦遠乎？以漢言之，高帝之時，叔孫通因秦樂人作宗廟樂，唐山夫人因帝好楚聲作房中樂。至武帝東封泰山，還坐明堂，其臣兒寬又請作神樂焉。以唐言之，高祖定天下，命祖孝孫等作雅樂；太宗平東都，破宋金剛等，作凱樂；至高宗時，景雲見，河水清，其臣張文收又作燕樂焉。迨至有宋，乾德樂作於太祖，太常和峴之所定也；萬國朝天樂、平晉樂作於太宗，郊廟祭享之所用也。至仁宗，因王堯臣之請，則又有大安樂、大晟樂焉。凡若此者，或襲先代之弊陋，或宣一時之侈心，先後一律也。夫數君之樂非出於崇德，則其和平天下，不徒無其本，亦且無其具矣。若乃諧
translation_en:
…Although the meanings of their names have not been transmitted, the purpose of exalting virtue was the same for the earlier and later sages, as we may readily imagine. Since the music of these several sages all served to exalt virtue, their efforts to bring harmony and peace to all under Heaven possessed not merely the instruments for doing so, but indeed the foundation.

From the Han to the Tang, and from the Tang to the Song, no dynasty lacked men who established rites and composed music. Yet were they not far removed from the sages? To speak of the Han: in Emperor Gao’s time, Shusun Tong employed musicians of the Qin to compose music for the ancestral temple, while Lady Tangshan composed music for the inner chambers because the emperor liked the sounds of Chu. When Emperor Wu performed the feng sacrifice in the east at Mount Tai and returned to take his seat in the Hall of Enlightenment, his minister Ni Kuan further requested that music for the spirits be composed. To speak of the Tang: after Gaozu pacified all under Heaven, he commanded Zu Xiaosun and others to compose elegant music. When Taizong subdued the Eastern Capital and defeated Song Jingang and others, triumphal music was composed. In Gaozong’s time, auspicious clouds appeared and the waters of the Yellow River ran clear; his minister Zhang Wenshou then composed banquet music.

Coming to the Song, the Qiande music was composed under Taizu and determined by He Xian of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. The music of “The Myriad States Pay Court to the Son of Heaven” and “Pacifying Jin” was composed under Taizong and used in sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples. Under Renzong, at Wang Yaochen’s request, there was also the music of “Great Peace” and “Great Splendor.” All such works either perpetuated the defects and crudities of preceding ages or expressed the extravagant desires of a particular time: earlier and later examples were all alike.

Since the music of these several rulers did not arise from exalting virtue, their efforts to bring harmony and peace to all under Heaven lacked not only the foundation but even the instruments for doing so. As for harmonizing [?]…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
儒之得失則亦有可言者王朴之所定以
鍾律為本盖取聲感於物而反感於人也
宋李照病其太高從而下其聲焉然鑄工
受賂而照莫之辨則其失在照矣范鎮之
所論以秬黍定律盖取黍實管中而斷之
為寸也司馬光惡其太拘從而議其失焉
然尺長丈二而鎮莫之察則其失在鎮矣
陳暘著樂書二百卷俗胡歌舞無所不有
優伶雜戲無所不載蕪穢褻嫚吾何觀焉
===
其惟蔡元定之律呂新書乎朱子稱其明
白淵潔縝密通暢九分一寸之說則淮南
太史可推五聲二變之數則杜氏通典可
考黃鍾圓徑本於漢斛之法損分變徵非調
本於孔氏之禮疏而先求聲氣之源因律
以生尺尤所謂卓然有見者盖鑿鑿乎其
可用也嗟夫樂之為用大矣哉可以治心
可以修身可以齊家可以治國可以平天
下古之聖帝明王所以使和氣薰蒸而天

儒之得失則亦有可言者 王朴之所定以
鍾律爲本蓋取聲感於物而反感於人也
宋李照病其太高從而下其聲焉然鑄工
受賂而照莫之辨則其失在照矣范鎮之
所論以秬黍定律蓋取黍實管中而斷之
爲寸也司馬光惡其太拘從而議其失焉
然尺長丈二而鎮莫之察則其失在鎮矣
陳暘著樂書二百卷俗胡歌舞無所不有
優伶雜戲無所不載蕪穢褻嫚吾何觀焉
===
其惟蔡元定之律呂新書乎朱子稱其明
白淵潔縝密通暢九分一寸之說則淮南
太史可推五聲二變之數則杜氏通典可
考黃鍾圓徑本於漢斛之法候分變徵非
本於孔氏之禮疏而先求聲氣之源因律
以生尺尤所謂卓然有見者蓋鑿鑿乎甚
可用也嗟夫樂之爲用大矣哉可以治心
可以修身可以齊家可以治國可以平天
下古之聖帝明王所以使和氣薰蒸而天
punctuated:
儒之得失，則亦有可言者。王朴之所定，以鍾律為本，盖取聲感於物而反感於人也。宋李照病其太高，從而下其聲焉。然鑄工受賂，而照莫之辨，則其失在照矣。范鎮之所論，以秬黍定律，盖取黍實管中而斷之為寸也。司馬光惡其太拘，從而議其失焉。然尺長丈二，而鎮莫之察，則其失在鎮矣。陳暘著《樂書》二百卷，俗胡歌舞，無所不有；優伶雜戲，無所不載。蕪穢褻嫚，吾何觀焉？
其惟蔡元定之《律呂新書》乎！朱子稱其明白淵潔，縝密通暢。九分一寸之說，則淮南、太史可推；五聲二變之數，則杜氏《通典》可考。黃鍾圓徑，本於漢斛之法；損分變徵非調，本於孔氏之《禮疏》。而先求聲氣之源，因律以生尺，尤所謂卓然有見者，盖鑿鑿乎其可用也。嗟夫！樂之為用大矣哉！可以治心，可以修身，可以齊家，可以治國，可以平天下。古之聖帝明王所以使和氣薰蒸而天
translation_en:
…As for the merits and faults of the scholars, there is also something to be said. Wang Pu based his determinations on the pitch standards of bells, taking sound to act upon things and, in turn, upon human beings. Li Zhao of the Song considered these pitches too high and accordingly lowered them. But the founders accepted bribes, and Zhao failed to detect this; the fault therefore lay with Zhao. Fan Zhen proposed determining pitch standards by means of black millet, filling pitch pipes with the grain and dividing the resulting measure into inches. Sima Guang considered this too restrictive and criticized its shortcomings. Yet the foot-rule measured one zhang and two chi [?], and Zhen failed to notice; the fault therefore lay with Zhen. Chen Yang wrote the Book of Music in two hundred juan. It included every sort of popular and foreign song and dance and recorded every sort of theatrical entertainment by performers. Rank, impure, profane, and disrespectful—what is there in it for me to study?
Surely the worthy work is Cai Yuanding’s New Book on the Pitch Standards! Master Zhu praised it as clear, profound, pure, meticulous, and lucid. Its account of nine fen constituting one cun can be traced through the writings of Huainan and the Grand Historian; its numerical treatment of the five notes and two altered notes can be examined in Master Du’s Comprehensive Institutions. Its account of the circular diameter of the Yellow Bell pitch pipe rests on the method of the Han hu measure; its treatment of fractional reductions and of the altered zhi note not constituting a mode [?] rests on Master Kong’s Subcommentary on the Rites. Above all, it first seeks the source of sound and vital breath and derives the foot-rule from the pitch standards. This is what may be called outstanding insight; its practical applicability is firmly established. Ah, how great are the uses of music! Through it one can order the mind, cultivate oneself, regulate the family, govern the state, and bring peace to all under Heaven. It was through this that the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity caused harmonious vital breath to pervade all, and Heaven…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
地位萬物育神祇格鳥獸馴者恃此而已
然而又在於天子建中和之極兼總條貫
金聲而玉振之此則愚所謂和平天下之
本也若乃制度文為則蔡氏之律呂新書
盖庶幾焉誠得精於其術者舉而用之則
優柔平中古樂復見於今日而致治不患
不如唐虞三代矣參酌百王之樂以成一
代之制計無出於此者執事倘與其進尚
當為
===
明天子言之
第三問
歐陽旦
同考試官右給事中張批〔歷論前代教〕
〔養以躬行心得四字貫串首尾剖析抑揚明白切當推〕
〔而行之必有裨於〕
聖化萬一
同考試官脩撰林批〔五策中間舉事實〕
〔殆無或遺處時務卓有所見而此一篇歷陳古今〕

同考試官脩撰林　批〔五策中間舉事實殆無或遺處時務卓有所見而此一篇歷陳古今〕
punctuated:
地位，萬物育，神祇格，鳥獸馴者，恃此而已。然而又在於天子建中和之極，兼總條貫，金聲而玉振之，此則愚所謂和平天下之本也。若乃制度文為，則蔡氏之《律呂新書》盖庶幾焉。誠得精於其術者舉而用之，則優柔平中，古樂復見於今日，而致治不患不如唐虞三代矣。參酌百王之樂，以成一代之制，計無出於此者。執事倘與其進，尚當為明天子言之。
第三問
歐陽旦
同考試官右給事中張批〔歷論前代教〕〔養，以躬行心得四字貫串首尾，剖析抑揚，明白切當，推〕〔而行之，必有裨於〕聖化萬一。
同考試官脩撰林批〔五策中間舉事實〕〔殆無或遺，處時務卓有所見，而此一篇歷陳古今〕
translation_en:
…earth takes its proper place, the myriad things flourish, the spirits of heaven and earth draw near, and birds and beasts become tame: all this depends upon music alone. Yet it also rests upon the Son of Heaven establishing the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony, comprehensively ordering its principles and particulars, and bringing them together as bells initiate the music and jade chimes complete it. This is what I humbly call the foundation for bringing peace and harmony to all under Heaven. As for its institutions, regulations, and ceremonial forms, Master Cai’s New Treatise on Pitch-Pipes (Lülü xinshu) comes close to meeting the need. If someone truly proficient in its methods could be found to put them into practice, ancient music, gentle, balanced, and harmonious, would appear again today. There would then be no fear that the resulting government would fall short of that of Tang and Yu or the Three Dynasties. To weigh and draw upon the music of the many past kings and establish the institutions of our own dynasty, no plan surpasses this. If you, sir, should approve this submission, I would further ask you to speak of it to the enlightened Son of Heaven.
Third Policy Question
Ouyang Dan
Associate Examiner Zhang, Right Supervising Secretary, comments: 〔The essay surveys the teaching〕〔and nurturing of earlier dynasties, threading the four characters “personal practice and inward understanding” through it from beginning to end. Its analysis and critical assessments are clear and apt. If its proposals were extended〕〔and put into practice, they would surely contribute〕some small measure to Your Majesty’s sagely transforming influence.
Associate Examiner Lin, Senior Compiler, comments: 〔Across the five policy essays, the historical facts cited〕〔leave almost nothing out. In addressing current affairs, the author displays outstanding insight; and this particular essay sets forth in succession, from antiquity to the present…〕

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
教養之道尤為詳悉非積學有素者不能也
考試官學士王批策以教化立說甚當末歸
之崇重師儒可謂有識之士
考試官學士徐批人材治道所繫此策能推
其本原而斟酌其所當行者甚有可觀是宜錄出以示
夫為師儒者
治化之隆必由夫人才之盛人才之盛必
由夫教養之深甚矣教養人才不可無其
具尤不可無其本也然有躬行心得以為
===
本有詩書禮樂以為具則又何患乎人才
之不盛治化之不隆也哉自昔聖王繼天
立極為億兆之君師任億兆之教養而司
徒之職典樂之官所由設也三代之隆其
法寢備天子公卿率於上者皆躬行心得
之餘布於下者皆關睢麟趾之化當是時
也家有塾黨有庠術有序國有學故人人
全君子之行濟濟收多士之效若伊尹舉
於畝畝而為成湯之阿衡傅說舉於版築

punctuated:
教養之道，尤為詳悉，非積學有素者不能也。

考試官學士王批：策以教化立說，甚當。末歸之崇重師儒，可謂有識之士。

考試官學士徐批：人材，治道所繫。此策能推其本原，而斟酌其所當行者，甚有可觀。是宜錄出，以示夫為師儒者。

治化之隆，必由夫人才之盛；人才之盛，必由夫教養之深。甚矣，教養人才不可無其具，尤不可無其本也！然有躬行心得以為本，有詩書禮樂以為具，則又何患乎人才之不盛、治化之不隆也哉？自昔聖王繼天立極，為億兆之君師，任億兆之教養，而司徒之職、典樂之官所由設也。三代之隆，其法寢備。天子公卿率於上者，皆躬行心得之餘；布於下者，皆關睢麟趾之化。當是時也，家有塾，黨有庠，術有序，國有學，故人人全君子之行，濟濟收多士之效。若伊尹舉於畝畝，而為成湯之阿衡；傅說舉於版築
translation_en:
…the methods of educating and nurturing are discussed with particular thoroughness. This could only have been achieved by someone with a solid foundation of accumulated learning.

Comment by Examiner Academician Wang: This policy essay very appropriately bases its argument on moral transformation through education. It concludes by advocating reverence and esteem for Confucian teachers. Its author may indeed be called a man of discernment.

Comment by Examiner Academician Xu: Talented men are essential to good government. This policy essay traces the matter to its foundations and weighs what ought to be put into practice; there is much to admire in it. It should therefore be transcribed and shown to those who serve as Confucian teachers.

The flourishing of government and moral transformation must arise from an abundance of talented men; an abundance of talented men must arise from thorough education and nurture. How essential it is that the education and nurture of talent have the requisite means—and, still more, the requisite foundation! Yet if personal practice and understanding gained in the heart provide the foundation, and the Odes, Documents, rites, and music provide the means, what cause is there to fear that talent will not abound or that government and moral transformation will not flourish? From ancient times, sage kings succeeded Heaven and established the supreme standard, acting as rulers and teachers of the countless people and taking responsibility for their education and nurture. Hence the establishment of the office of Minister of Education and that of Director of Music. At the height of the Three Dynasties, these arrangements gradually became complete. The example set from above by the Son of Heaven, the dukes, and the ministers was entirely an outgrowth of their personal practice and inward understanding; what spread among those below was entirely the transforming influence exemplified by “The Ospreys” (Guan ju) and “The Qilin’s Hoofs” (Lin zhi). At that time, there were teaching rooms in residential groups, schools in neighborhoods, schools in districts, and academies in the capitals. Thus everyone fully attained the conduct of a gentleman, and the abundant ranks of worthy men bore fruit. For example, Yi Yin was raised from the fields [?] to become Cheng Tang’s chief minister, the A-heng; Fu Yue was raised from the work of building rammed-earth walls…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
而作商家之霖雨太公望舉於渭濱而著
鷹揚之偉烈盖以當時教無不周人無不
學豈詩文懿所謂學成而隱者非耶自時
厥後一壞於春秋之功利再壞於戰國之
縱橫蔓延至於秦火煨燼之餘聖賢學校
之教荒矣漢高帝不事詩書而所用之臣
若良平任智數蕭曹起刀筆其視教養為
何事然而豁達大度亦足以成一代之業
文帝未遑禮樂而所尚之人若鼂錯之明
===
申韓盖公之事黃老其視教養為何物然
而恭儉愛民亦足以成一時之治武帝勸
學興禮表章六經元帝雅尚儒術經生迭
相非不崇儒也然所崇者虛名而已故一
則窮奢極欲而致海內之虛耗一則優游
不斷以致漢業之寢衰躬行之實何有耶
明帝尊師重傅臨雍拜老唐太宗大召名
儒增廣生員非不務教也然所務者虛文
而已故一則天竺求書而啓異端之尚一

而作商家之霖雨，太公望舉於渭濱而著鷹揚之偉烈。盖以當時教無不周，人無不學，豈詩文懿所謂學成而隱者非耶？自時厥後，一壞於春秋之功利，再壞於戰國之縱橫，蔓延至於秦火煨燼之餘，聖賢學校之教荒矣。
漢高帝不事詩書，而所用之臣，若良平任智數，蕭曹起刀筆，其視教養為何事？然而豁達大度，亦足以成一代之業。文帝未遑禮樂，而所尚之人，若鼂錯之明申韓，盖公之事黃老，其視教養為何物？然而恭儉愛民，亦足以成一時之治。武帝勸學興禮，表章六經；元帝雅尚儒術，經生迭相，非不崇儒也。然所崇者虛名而已，故一則窮奢極欲而致海內之虛耗，一則優游不斷以致漢業之寢衰，躬行之實何有耶？明帝尊師重傅，臨雍拜老；唐太宗大召名儒，增廣生員，非不務教也。然所務者虛文而已，故一則天竺求書而啓異端之尚，一
translation_en:
…and became the sustaining rain of the Shang house; Taigong Wang was raised from the banks of the Wei River and achieved mighty deeds, soaring like an eagle. This was because instruction then reached everywhere and everyone learned. Were these not men who, as Shi Wenyi [?] put it, had completed their learning and withdrawn into seclusion? Thereafter, this order was first undermined by the pursuit of achievement and profit in the Spring and Autumn period, and again by the competing alliances of the Warring States period. The damage spread until, amid the ashes left by the Qin book burning, the instruction of sages and worthies through schools had fallen into neglect.
Emperor Gao of Han did not devote himself to the Odes and the Documents. Among the ministers he employed, Zhang Liang and Chen Ping relied on clever stratagems, while Xiao He and Cao Can rose from clerical work. What importance did he attach to educating and nurturing the people? Yet his open-mindedness and magnanimity sufficed to establish a dynasty. Emperor Wen had no leisure for rites and music. Among those he esteemed were Chao Cuo, versed in the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, and Master Gai, devoted to those of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi. What value did he place on educating and nurturing the people? Yet his reverence, frugality, and love for the people sufficed to bring good government in his time. Emperor Wu encouraged learning, promoted ritual, and gave prominence to the Six Classics. Emperor Yuan greatly esteemed Confucian learning, and classical scholars served successively as chief ministers. It was not that they failed to honor Confucianism. Yet what they honored was merely its empty reputation. Thus the former exhausted the resources of the realm through extravagant luxury and unbridled desires, while the latter, through irresolution and indecision, caused the gradual decline of the Han enterprise. Where was the substance of putting learning into personal practice? Emperor Ming honored teachers and tutors, visited the imperial academy, and bowed to the elders. Emperor Taizong of Tang summoned eminent Confucian scholars in great numbers and increased the number of students. It was not that they failed to attend to education. Yet what they attended to was merely empty form. Thus the former sought scriptures in Tianzhu, opening the way to esteem for heterodox teachings, while the latter…

title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
則閨門慙德而貽雜夷之譏正心之學何
有耶噫教化如斯大抵無其本矣漢之治
所以止於漢唐之治所以止於唐而不敢
上擬三代之萬一者有由然也迨夫有宋
學校之興始於仁宗慶曆之詔而韓范諸
賢以道相濟人才於是乎盛矣自後胡安
定教授蘇湖立經義治事齋以訓諸生其
體則仁義禮樂其文則詩書史傳其用則
澤潤生民歸于皇極故出其門者淵篤如
===
錢藻純明如孫覺直溫如范純仁簡諒如
錢公輔人才表表見重于時三代以下教
化之行僅見于此我
國家自有天下以來崇儒重道
列聖一心建學立師四方承式厚澤深仁與兩
儀而同化良法美意垂萬載而無疆今日
之學校三代之學校也今日之人才三代
之人才也今日之治化三代之治化也自
非有其本而又有其具何以能致若是之

國家自有天下以來崇儒重道
列聖一心建學立師九門承式厚澤深仁與兩
儀而同化良法美意垂萬載而無疆今日
之學校三代之學校也今日之人才三代

非青其本而又有其具何以能致若是之

…the other brought shame upon his virtue in his domestic affairs, inviting criticism that he had mingled with the barbarians. What learning aimed at rectifying the mind was there in this? Alas! Education and moral transformation of this sort largely lacked their foundation. There was a reason why Han governance never surpassed that of the Han, and Tang governance never surpassed that of the Tang, so that neither could presume to compare itself with even a ten-thousandth part of the achievement of the Three Dynasties.
With the advent of the Song, the flourishing of schools began with Emperor Renzong’s edict of the Qingli era. Worthies such as Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan supported one another through the Way, and men of talent consequently flourished. Subsequently, Hu Anding taught in Suzhou and Huzhou, establishing halls for classical interpretation and practical administration to instruct his students. The substance of his teaching was benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music; its textual materials were the Book of Odes, the Book of Documents, histories, and biographies; its practical application was to bestow benefits upon the people and bring them into accord with the sovereign’s ultimate standard. Thus, among those who studied under him were Qian Zao, profound and steadfast; Sun Jue, pure and discerning; Fan Chunren, upright and gentle; and Qian Gongfu, straightforward and trustworthy. These outstanding men of talent were highly esteemed in their time. Since the Three Dynasties, such effective education and moral transformation had scarcely been seen elsewhere.
Ever since our dynasty gained possession of All under Heaven, it has honored Confucian learning and esteemed the Way. Successive sage emperors have been of one mind, establishing schools and appointing teachers, with all regions following their example. Their abundant beneficence and profound benevolence work transformation together with Heaven and Earth; their excellent institutions and fine intentions endure without limit through ten thousand years. The schools of today are the schools of the Three Dynasties; the men of talent of today are the men of talent of the Three Dynasties; the governance and moral transformation of today are the governance and moral transformation of the Three Dynasties. 皇上求賢之盛心而無負矣

作者槩有可取而此一策所謂區處之法變通之要皆鑿鑿可行
信非迂腐者所及主司得此薦拔何疑
觀子厚乾父坤母之論則知天下之大無
一事而非吾之所當為觀希文先憂後樂
之言則知天下之事無一時而非吾之所
當慮是故雖賤在匹夫而所以堯舜君民

嘗以是展轉於胷中矣請一為執事陳之
且夫地之與民相須為用民非地無以盡
其力地非民無以盡其利今蘇松嘉湖諸
郡介在東南為南畿之近輔考之禹貢即

Examiner, Academician Xu, comments: His learning is comprehensive and perceptive, and his literary talent ample and unhurried [?]. What appears in his writings is generally commendable. In this particular policy essay, the proposed methods of managing affairs and essentials of adapting to circumstances are all demonstrably practicable—truly beyond the reach of pedantic scholars. Having found such a candidate, how could the presiding examiners hesitate to recommend and advance him?
Reading Zihou’s discussion of Qian as father and Kun as mother, one understands that, throughout the vast realm, there is no undertaking that is not our duty to perform. Reading Xiwen’s words about being first to worry and last to enjoy happiness, one understands that there is no moment when the affairs of the realm should not concern us. Thus, even in the humble position of a commoner, bringing ruler and people to the standard of Yao and Shun has never fallen outside one’s allotted duties. How, then, could one admonish oneself against thoughts that go beyond one’s station? You have posed a policy question concerning tribute and taxation in the southeast and troops and their provisions in the northeast, graciously consulting us students and wishing to hear appropriate ways of managing these matters and adapting to circumstances. These are great questions of state, which cannot be called minor matters of court deliberation. I, an unworthy student, have also repeatedly turned them over in my mind. Allow me to set them forth for you.
Land and people depend upon each other to serve their purposes. Without land, people cannot fully employ their labor; without people, land cannot fully yield its benefits. The prefectures of Suzhou, Songjiang, Jiaxing, and Huzhou lie in the southeast and form the nearby supporting region of the Southern Metropolitan Area. title: 成化十七年會試錄
text:
聞有殷富之稱也今之地即禹貢之地今
之民非禹貢之民矣自東晉南宋之遷安
生齒日聚以繁又況我
朝氣化之隆經制之備雞鳴犬吠之聲至遍
達乎四境桑麻之密寸土不遺耕織之勤
卒歲不已物產安得而不盛乎故其地號
為都會而穀粟布帛之出甲於天下
朝廷上供之需十當八九瑶琨篠簜之屬何
足言耶此則民力有以盡地利也然土地

乎茲欲為之區處則不可不求其弊之所
在而革之豪強兼并宜稍倣限田之制侈
靡浮費宜申明違式之條寬雜泛之征懲

使訟訐不作水旱無虞則庶幾其可耳至

… been described as affluent. The land today is the same land as in the Tribute of Yu, but its people are no longer those of the Tribute of Yu. Since the Eastern Jin and Southern Song relocated and settled here, the population has grown ever more numerous. Moreover, under our dynasty, the transforming influence of harmonious vital forces flourishes, and institutions and regulations are fully established. The sounds of crowing cocks and barking dogs reach every corner; mulberry and hemp grow so densely that not an inch of soil is left unused. Diligent plowing and weaving continue throughout the year. How could its produce fail to be abundant? Thus this region is known as a great center of population and commerce, and its output of grain, cloth, and silk ranks first in the realm. It meets eight or nine tenths of the court’s requirements for tribute supplies. What need is there even to mention such items as precious jades and fine and large bamboos? Here, human labor has indeed fully realized the land’s productive potential.
Yet what the land produces is limited, while public and private demands are endless. The extravagance of aristocratic idlers is a leaking vessel; the gradual encroachments of heterodox teachings are a bottomless drain. The people’s strength is consequently exhausted. Alas! Among the eight affairs of government in the Great Plan, food and wealth come first. When the people of the very region that supplies food and wealth are in such a condition, how can we fail to be concerned? To devise arrangements for them now, we must identify the sources of these abuses and eliminate them. We should ease miscellaneous levies and punish [?] corrupt officials who prey upon the people. We should also rectify field boundaries and improve water management, so that lawsuits and accusations do not arise and there is no fear of floods or drought. Then we might come close to a workable solution. As for …
