山東、河南二省，雄峙東北，為京畿之近輔。考之《春秋》，即齊、魯、宋、陳、鄭、衛之墟。當時兵車四出，邦賦荐增，未聞有困憊之憂也。今之地即春秋之地，今之民非春秋之民矣。自五胡、遼、金之擾攘，而生齒日耗以寡。迨至我朝，氣化之盛，安養之深，獸蹄鳥跡之道始不交於國中。然太平既久，民不知兵，游惰漸生，野多曠土，民物安得而大盛乎？故其地雖號大藩，而食常不足以給兵，兵常不足以衛農，百里千乘之富奚可言邪？此則民力未能盡地力也。夫生之者既不足，奪之者又不巳，流離□□於凶年，逋竄相仍於苛政，而民物益敝矣。嗚呼！孔子言政：「足食，□兵。」以兵食所出之地，而其民若此，又能不慮之乎？茲欲為之變通，則不可不究其
translation_en:
…to speak of what is most essential, does it not also rest with those above to curtail expenditure so that the people may prosper? The Analects says: “If the common people have enough, how could their ruler alone lack enough?” This is what it means.

The two provinces of Shandong and Henan stand majestically in the northeast, serving as nearby supports to the capital region. Examined against the Spring and Autumn Annals, they occupy the former territories of Qi, Lu, Song, Chen, Zheng, and Wei. In those days, war chariots went forth in every direction and state levies repeatedly increased, yet we hear of no concern about exhaustion and distress. The land today is the land of the Spring and Autumn period, but the population today is no longer that of the Spring and Autumn period. From the upheavals of the Five Hu, the Liao, and the Jin onward, the population dwindled day by day. Only under our dynasty, with its flourishing civilizing influence and profound care for the people's peaceful sustenance, did trails of beasts' hoofprints and birds' tracks cease to crisscross the realm. Yet peace has now endured so long that the people know nothing of warfare; idleness has gradually arisen, and much land lies uncultivated. How, then, could the people and their material resources flourish greatly? Thus, although these lands are called great provincial bulwarks, their grain is constantly insufficient to provision the troops, and their troops are constantly insufficient to protect the farmers. How can one speak of the wealth of a domain a hundred li across with a thousand chariots? Here, the people's productive capacity has failed to realize the land's full potential.

Those who produce are already insufficient, while those who take from them never cease. In years of famine, the people are displaced [two illegible characters]; under harsh government, flight and concealment follow one another without end, and the people and their resources become still more depleted. Alas! Speaking of government, Confucius said: “Make food sufficient; [make sufficient?] the troops.” When the people fare thus in the very lands that supply soldiers and provisions, how can we fail to be concerned? 傳潮
punctuated:
害之所在而去之。孱弱濫於行伍，必時其簡閱之令；精強役於私門，必嚴其鬻放之律。招集流亡，咸復其故業；懲艾游惰，悉勤於恒產。而又為之廣屯田，厚儲畜，使兵寓於農，食常有備，則庶幾其可耳。至於極其要而言之，又在於上之省事以安民乎！記曰：「庶民安，故財用足；財用足，故百志成。」此之謂也。雖然，張詠拔茶植桑，則成都之富庶可以並美于上國；趙充國按兵屯田，則金城之兵食可以屈服乎叛羌。政之待人也，固如此。區處變通之宜，既如前所陳矣，盍亦求其人如趙、張者，重其任而責其成乎？區區管見，惟執事擇焉。

第五問
傅潮

同考試官主事吳批：〔此策欲觀士子時務〕以收俊傑。是答措置四者之弊，有識見，有考據。若良醫治病，藥不虛投，救弊之方恐不出此。健羨！健羨！
translation_en:
…where the harm lies, and eliminate it. Where the weak and unfit indiscriminately fill the ranks, orders for inspection and selection must be carried out at the proper times; where strong, capable soldiers serve private households, the laws against selling releases from service must be rigorously enforced. Gather back those who have fled or wandered away, restoring all to their former livelihoods; chastise the idle and indolent, making all diligently pursue settled occupations. Furthermore, expand agricultural garrisons and build up reserves, so that soldiers are incorporated into farming and provisions are always available. Then there may be some prospect of success. To state the essential point, does it not also depend upon those above reducing their demands so that the people may live in peace? The Record of Rites says: “When the common people are at peace, financial resources are sufficient; when financial resources are sufficient, all aspirations can be fulfilled.” This is what it means.

Nevertheless, when Zhang Yong uprooted tea plants and planted mulberries, Chengdu’s wealth and population could rival those of the central regions; when Zhao Chongguo held his troops in place and established agricultural garrisons, the troops and provisions of Jincheng could bring the rebellious Qiang into submission. Such indeed is government’s dependence upon the right men. The appropriate arrangements and adaptations have already been set out above. Why not also seek men like Zhao and Zhang, entrust them with weighty responsibilities, and hold them accountable for success? These are merely my limited views; I leave it to you, sir, to choose what is useful.

Fifth Question
Fu Chao

Associate Examiner Zeng, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “Among the answers to this policy question in the examination hall, most treat the methods for handling the four matters in general terms. An essay like this, whose proposals are apt and clearly practicable, is truly hard to find.”

Associate Examiner Li, a Hanlin Expositor, comments: “For a scholar to be able to discuss the great affairs of the realm in this way is remarkable. As for his entering government service … [?] he ought to be recommended.”

Associate Examiner Chen, a Hanlin Expositor, comments: “A policy question on current affairs serves precisely to reveal learning suited to practical service. This essay’s plans are orderly, and its breadth and depth [?] are apparent.”

Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: “There is planning and there is insight, and the writing adequately conveys them. This deserves to be selected for inclusion.”

Examiner Xu, a Hanlin Academician, comments: “Long-established practices inevitably develop abuses. If these proposals were adopted, reform would still be possible. The essay concludes by returning to the importance of personnel. Though this may seem commonplace, nothing goes beyond it as the essential principle of government. Readers must take care not to disregard it.”

A long-established administration inevitably has policies that merely follow precedent; those who govern must have appropriate means of adapting to change. Once a policy has been established, over time it comes to be treated carelessly; such carelessness gives abuses an opening to arise. This [illegible] is why those who govern must modify and adapt it, bringing it into accord with the needs of the time. Policies will thereby be put in order, and the proper way of governing will continually be maintained. You gentlemen presiding over the examination have posed policy questions at the spring Metropolitan Examination, taking matters of the realm that are great and [illegible] and graciously putting them to us students. Surely you expect us to possess talents fit for practical service. How could I dare not exhaust my humble understanding in reply?
